#9185. Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

Visitors to the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach interact with a sculpture by the collective MSCHF on the Perrotin stand Photo: Liliana Mora

As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”

#9184. MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years

The 200-work exhibition will open in December 2027, almost a year after the closing of the Tate Modern’s current retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist.

The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in New York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years.

MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.

Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and Afro-Caribbean divinity, natural reclamation and life cycles, and the deconstruction of borders.

Presaging Mendieta's groundbreaking Siluetas were transgressive performance pieces centering the use of blood as a signifier of violence, fertility, vitality, and ancestral ritual. Her 1973 performance “Untitled (Rape Scene)” and its photo documentation were created in response to the rape and murder of 20-year-old University of Iowa student Sarah Ann Ottens, whereas her filmed performance of “Untitled (Death of a Chicken)” (1972) graphically referenced animal sacrifice practices associated with Santería.

The retrospective also centers the artist's lens-based work, her sustained interest in organic material, and how her travels, reunion with Cuba, and art residencies sparked major evolutions in her practice. Mendieta's 1981 Esculturas Rupestres (Rupestrian Sculptures) series, 1983–85 fellowship at the American Academy in Rome, and a variety of later works, including a series of ink-wash drawings, are among the highlights mentioned by the museum.

“Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” said Beverly Adams, MoMA's Latin American art curator and retrospective co-organizer, in a press statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.”

In celebrating Mendieta's punctuated career, the retrospective apparently strays away from the tragic circumstances of the 36-year-old artist's death and the unshakeable speculations that continue to follow. Such is the case with Mendieta's ongoing exhibition at the Tate Modern, which also omitted mentioning the artist's death and the resulting controversy surrounding her husband, artist Carl Andre.

Nevertheless, the artist's own poignant grapplings with loss and rebirth are staged independently of the discourse, underscoring her persisting critical impact in a visual arts landscape that has rarely offered credit to women artists.

Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective will be on view at MoMA from December 12, 2027 to April 15, 2028.

#9183. Shisuo Design Office creates "surreal" rural house in China using salvaged steel

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the new one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” said Shisuo Design Office.

“Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio said.

Externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” said the studio.

“For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

#9181. Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89

In this column honoring those we lost in the art world, we also remember a British painter of bewitching scenes and one of Japan’s greatest manga artists.

In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year.

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."

#9179. A Marquee Week of Indulgence

The latest from the fall auctions, museum protests, and tackling the British Empire one video at a time.

My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work, alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution.

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.

On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the Museum of Modern Art during an annual benefit for the museum’s Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center last Thursday, calling on filmmaker and honored guest Steven Spielberg to reject the recognition and boycott the museum over Leon Black’s Epstein-related sexual abuse allegations. Cold, biting rain soaked the group of 20 artists and activists outside the gala, and Spielberg hasn’t acknowledged their demands.

All things considered, Iraqi-British data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi’s first-ever book, which was released last week, comes at a most opportune time. The book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026), comes from Chalabi five-year endeavor in examining class inequality in the United States by analyzing the incomes, expenses, tax deductions, systemic barriers, and livelihoods of 10 Americans across the nation. In a recent interview with Hyperallergic’s Lakshmi Rivera Amin, Chalabi noted that journalists themselves often don’t acknowledge or even recognize how their own class upbringing can color their reporting on wealth and poverty, whereas other markers like race and gender are positioned as lenses of understanding.

A new video exhibition on the High Line also tackles greed and indulgence through the lens of the British Empire’s storied trade monopolies and resource theft across South Asia and China. Works by Shahzia Sikander and the artist duo Hylozoic/Desires unpack the British stronghold on salt in India and the empire’s deliberate opium influx in China during the Qing dynasty, while also highlighting historic and speculative subversions that disrupt dominant colonial narratives.

I wasn’t super fond of the High Line’s most recent film installation, but this one sounds more up my alley on a subjective, personal history level. I’m looking forward to checking it out soon — before the weather really turns south — and visiting the Mighty Miniatures exhibition that’s opening this Saturday at the National Museum of the American Indian.

#9178. Is My Art Funny to You?

A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, artist and chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 is a worthy upgrade to its predecessor, cleverly interlinking back and lumbar systems so you're completely supported as you move around in the chair. It's still not the most attractive of chairs, and assembly could be more straightforward, but once it's up and running, you'll find levels of ergonomics that actually belie its $499.99 / £459.99 price.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Chairs seem to come in pairs. I've been getting a lot of chairs in for review recently, with the remarkably similar Secretlab Titan Evo and the DXRacer Martian Pro showing up around the same time. Now, having just reviewed the Boulies EP600, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 has taken my focus – and they have so much in common, it’s like they were separated at birth.

The design of the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 is almost a mirror image of the Boulies EP600: Both feature curvy three-piece back panels with responsive lumbar supports, pull-out footrests, and they’re roughly the same price. But where the Boulies EP600 was feature-packed and poorly executed, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 nails the execution, and it’s definitely one of the best office chairs for back pain. It’s also a marked improvement on its predecessor, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro.

Like most of Sihoo’s chairs, the Doro C300 Pro makes use of mesh throughout. There’s nothing wrong with that: mesh makes chairs lighter and easier to pack, but it lacks the sink-in sumptuousness of cushioned chairs, including its own budget-friendly Sihoo M18.

However, where the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro gets everything absolutely right is in its engineering. While it can feel a little clunky and firm to start with, once it’s dialled-in it reaches astonishing levels of comfort with the versatility to move around and change positions.

This begins with the lumbar support, which naturally moves and follows your lower back as you lean backwards and forwards. Unlike the aggressive system in the Boulies EP600, it flows with you and never becomes intrusive.

Sihoo also includes a sacral support system here, which cradles the heart-shaped sacrum bone at the base of your spine with a gentle pressure I’ve never felt before. It’s one of the best lumbar systems I’ve used, and it’s adjustable so you can hone it just as you want it.

The lumbar support moves alongside the rest of the chair as you shift around; lean back and the armrests follow the backrest and the seat cushion moves forwards. It's always got your back (literally), and it delivers on the promise that the automated Hbada X7 failed to deliver, and it does so without motors or AI.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Endless adjustments don’t end there: the armrests can also be tweaked and rotated to optimise your comfort levels, apparently through eight dimensions. This sounds like it might break the very fabric of reality, but if I’m going to implode with an alternative-dimension version of myself, at least I can do so with comfortable elbows.

One neat feature here is that the rear portion of the armrests flips up and locks into place, giving you a little more comfort when you’re reading, sketching, or diving back into another 16-hour GTA VI binge, and the (optional) mesh leg rest also helps you relax into a state of utter relaxation as you cause chaos in Vice City.

Sihoo reckons the chair will suit anyone up to 6’ 3”, and it fits my 6’ 4” height perfectly, with the headrest in just the right place. Sihoo has also upgraded the weight accommodation to a maximum of 136 kg, so this is a chair that can be used by pretty much anybody and everybody.

Beren’s take on the original C300 Pro was that it was one ugly motherfu…rniture. The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 doesn’t break the mould in terms of looks, and it’s almost indistinguishable from other ultra-adjustable ergonomic office chairs: it’s the Boulies EP600, it’s the Hinomi H2 Pro.

These chairs tend to be triumphs of function over form, although I’m not sure anyone outside of Gold's Gym will have shoulders wide enough to justify the upper width of the backrest. Where they differentiate themselves is in the view from the back.

The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 looks reasonably attractive: the headrest’s large “eyes” and its nose-like supports actually recall Gonzo a little bit, while the armrests, in grey, have a friendly cetacean look about them. It’s still not the best-looking chair, but these touches add a playfulness that reduces its dour, generic design.

Choosing the grey colourway Sihoo sent us also helps lighten the heaviness of the design and stops it looking like a predatory black blob in front of your desk.

Take note: this is a herculean, 27kg chair that comes in two boxes, and not something you’ll want to be moving vertically once assembled. Within one of those boxes you’ll also find my pet peeve with Sihoo chairs: having to put the base together and insert those 10 screws. I’ve done it countless times and it never gets easier or more fun. It makes me think about my own mortality.

Sihoo’s assembly process is nowhere near as straightforward as, say, Branch’s. There is a fair amount of cross-referencing to be done between the manual, the screw blister-pack, and the chair itself, to the extent that I thought an escape room-style door would open somewhere when I’d completed it. The armrests connect via washers that seem a little too big for their holes, and they take a bit of brute force to get them in place.

Sihoo has kept the number of steps involved to the absolute minimum, and when it’s done it feels remarkably sturdy. But the niggling annoyances in its construction do add up, and it feels like there are plenty of opportunities for Sihoo to simplify things. They can start with that wretched base.

Office chair pricing is so complicated and fluid that it can be hard to find a coherent and consistent price, but apparently the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 carries an RRP of $499.99 / £409.99, with the footrest costing an extra $40 / £50, but these prices are often discounted. The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V1 was a frankly absurd RRP of $699 when Beren reviewed it; thankfully, Sihoo seems to have made its pricing more sensible since then.

Is it worth it? I’d say a definite yes; despite my grumbles about the construction process, this is a comfortable and innovative chair that gets a lot of things right. If you’re torn between the Sihoo Doro Pro C300 V2 and the Boulies EP600 ($489.99 / £429.99) I’d definitely recommend the Sihoo option.

If your budget stretches a little more, then the Hinomi H2 Pro ($ / £759) is a worthy contender, with similar adjustability and a neat folding feature — although it lacks the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2’s versatile armrests. And, of course, there’s the ever-dependable Sihoo M18 (under $ / £200), if you want to spend less but still need a decent level of lumbar support.

Sihoo’s upgrades really do make a big difference with the Doro C300 Pro V2. The way it all works together is a marvel of engineering, and it adds up to one of the best back support systems I’ve ever used. The fact that it achieves it without batteries and motors is impressive in itself. It’s a chair that cradles your back from the moment you sit in it, but that can also be tweaked in just the right ways, without ever becoming overwhelming or overcomplicated.

The biggest downsides here are its chunky looks and its fiddly assembly process, but both of these will evaporate the moment you sit on it. It’s the perfect chair for people who like to move around a lot, and who like to kick back for entertainment in the same chair they work in.

With over 20 years of experience in journalism and content creation, Henry has covered everything from gaming and digital art to VFX, new tech and film. He loves to translate the complex into accessible, whether that with text or video. When he’s not thinking about what creatives need to do their jobs properly, he’s busy discovering new and creative ways to fall off his bicycle.

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

#9175. Nike Tuned Air "a huge stride forward" in air-filled trainer design says innovation lead

Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

“I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”

Tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” said McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

“At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” said McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”

“If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

“It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” said McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

“So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he said. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “important part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

“There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” said McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”

#9174. Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

Auctioneer Oliver Barker selling Blossoming Chestnut Trees on Wednesday, 18 November Courtesy Sotheby's

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's

Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's

One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a new auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

#9173. Recovering Edward Said’s Voice

Moustafa Bayoumi on a new documentary about the legendary Palestinian critic and activist; plus, can contemporary art make us laugh?

For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship. Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi

Is it a step too far for virtual branding?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best NHL logos are timeless, but the National Hockey League has been covering them up recently, at least on television broadcasts. After the addition of dynamic digital advertising on dashers and on the ice, the league's latest technological 'advance' is the use of digital overlays to replace real centre logos with temporary virtual ones.

Spectators in the arena see the home team's usual design, but viewers watching on TV are shown the team's Hometown Remix logo, a temporary alternate design being used for select games. It must have seemed like a great idea when it was floated, but it doesn't seem to be going down well with viewers, with some saying they'll stop watching if the practice continues.

@The_Mexinadian There’s already too much virtual crap on the ice and video as it is. Why do we need a HUGE fake logo that hurts my eyes whenever anyone skates over it?!November 15, 2026

Hometown Remix is a leaguewide campaign in which each team has a special-edition uniform featuring specifically local references. Many teams are using modified, throwback or entirely redesigned logos. The NHL says the campaign "uniquely and authentically celebrates the fans, fabric, and local culture of each NHL team and the cities they call home".

But in sports like the NHL, a logo design isn't just an identity, it's revenue. Multiple logos, throwback designs and temporary remixes all largely about selling a new range of merchandise. Putting a temporary logo on the ice becomes highly visible advertising for alternate jerseys. The problem is that it's appalling to look at.

The ice is *the* thing that immediately separates watching hockey from watching any other sport the instant you turn it on. It's beautiful and unique. Slapping giant fake digital novelty logos on top of the earnestly painted logos that are actually there is a shame. https://t.co/JvoXxCJWkONovember 13, 2026

You can literally see a white glow around every player at center ice??? How was this approvedNovember 18, 2026

WHAT IS THE POINT!?!?! https://t.co/GLRkQI5M30November 15, 2026

Some viewers already complained about the digitisation of adverts on dashers and on the ice to make them look more prominent. For some, the new virtual logos is the last straw, making the viewing experience feel detached from reality.

The lack of motion blur or shadows on the digital fake when players pass over the centre of the ice makes it look uncanny, as though players are passing in front of a badly keyed green screen. Any black in the design can make the puck momentarily disappear from view.

"When they brought in the digitally superimposed ads on the boards I stopped watching altogether. Too distracting and horribly done. I remember seeing players disappear into the ads," one person writes on X.

Some fans are concerned that the NHL's use of virtual team logos could be merely the start and that the league might be testing the ground to potentially replace team logos with sponsors. I'm not sure brands would want to be associated with the backlash that would cause.

Designers have to consider an increasingly wide range of potential digital applications for logo designs these days. On the ice in an NHL game probably shouldn't be one of them.

#9171. Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program

NYSS is now accepting applications from independent thinkers and experimenters in the arts.

What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking.

Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas.

The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language.

At the heart of the New York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to examine their work from multiple perspectives while developing the confidence and critical awareness to move their practice forward.

The curriculum combines independent studio work with intensive two-week Marathons, drawing courses, Critical Studies seminars, and encounters with visiting artists. The School’s renowned Evening Lecture Series and Exhibitions further connect students to a broad community of artists, writers, historians, and thinkers. Drawing remains a foundational component of the program, informing the study of painting and sculpture and encouraging deeper attention to perception, form, space, and material.

Students in the MFA program are encouraged to engage with the histories of art while questioning established conventions, exploring the relationships between representation and abstraction, and discovering new possibilities through sustained experimentation. The goal is to support the development of an independent, thoughtful, and resilient artistic practice. The MFA program’s second year culminates with a thesis project and exhibition in the School’s historic galleries, connecting a new generation of artists with a building that has been part of New York’s cultural life for more than a century.

For artists seeking a demanding, immersive environment in which to deepen their work, the New York Studio School offers an education built around the essential questions of art-making, and the time, community, and commitment needed to pursue them.

#9170. Photos reveal scale of Trump’s White House ballroom, drawing criticism

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump announced the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”

It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion said it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

The administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

#9169. Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory

Drawing on the work of artists and theorists alike, the art historian traces how generations of Black painters have deployed color and how color, in turn, shapes our understanding of Blackness.

Sometime in the 1980s, when I was still a fledgling curator of 20th-century art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, I was invited to the studio of a rather prominent artist. During our conversation, the work of Jacob Lawrence came up somehow, and the artist mentioned that he was impressed by what he described as Lawrence’s use of “Black” colors. Did I mention this artist was White?

I was gobsmacked by the comment. Not that I wasn’t attuned to stereotypical societal associations of color — most notably, of bright, loud colors with Black people. In the 1950s, a full three decades before Nancy Reagan practically made red her official color, my Aunt Ruth was appalled that my mother made red coats for my sister and me, rather than using more acceptable pastel colors. Then a friend who grew up in Northern Ireland told me that Protestant Irish factions associated Catholic Irish with loud and bright colors.

But how did such racially associative ideas translate to the realm of the so-called “fine” arts? I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026).

#9168. GTA 6 review: Holy sh*t it’s good
