Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Funny, sad, euphoric… GTA 6 is the most entertaining and emotionally engaging open world I’ve played. Rockstar has taken the sandbox freedom of Grand Theft Auto and the environmental storytelling of Red Dead Redemption 2 and made something that feels lived-in. The characters, humour, and systems are all wonderfully written, and the attention to detail makes Leonida a place I want to stay in long after I’d finished the story. The set pieces rival Hollywood, but I'll remember the small, unplanned moments.

An extraordinarily detailed, living open world

Jason and Lucia are brilliant protagonists

Hilarious, unpredictable emergent gameplay

Superb environmental storytelling and art direction

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In brief: 5/5. Grand Theft Auto VI (reviewed on PS5, out 19 November) is the most convincing open world I’ve played.

I laughed out loud multiple times within minutes of starting Grand Theft Auto VI. Not a chuckle or a smirk, but proper laughs, grinning ear to ear, as a particularly large resident of Leonida giggled, ran, stumbled, staggered and tripped over a railing into the river below. It was ridiculous and completely unexpected, and I loved it.

We've waited 13 years for GTA VI and from the opening credits, Rockstar has crafted a hyperreal but intensely personal world where every corner of Leonida and Vice City offers a surprise. I've been playing for three weeks, finished the story, seen some endings, and I'm still playing to find out what random secrets Leonida has left to share. Much of it has nothing to do with the fate of Lucia and Jason, GTA VI's modern-day Bonnie and Clyde. (Read our GTA VI coverage for more on the game.)

Driving around, you'll spot Just Stop Oil-style protests blocking traffic, teenagers dropping rocks onto motorway cars, or posters and flyers that lead to mysteries and new characters to call from your iFruit phone's contacts list. These aren't side quests in the traditional sense, with a marker on your map and a list to tick off; they're connections to random people, and the sense that this world exists beyond the screen.

Those teenagers dropping rocks? I detoured to teach them a lesson. Later, I stopped for someone posting for social media while balancing on a bridge, and failed to save him when he fell, and I actually felt bad. I pulled over for some teens daring each other to jump from a bridge into a river, decided to show them how it was done, and while I was swimming, they stole my car.

It's not risk and reward; it's just life in Leonida. It's incredibly fun.

The scale of GTA VI is incredible, but not in the usual sense of a vast map to cross. It's the depth and detail that gets me: the branding, signage, store shelves of snacks and comic books that can be read, snatches of conversations from passersby muttering about their lives or something they heard on the radio, the same thing I heard on the radio. Most buildings can be broken into and explored, and I've spent far too long sneaking into warehouses that have no obvious reason to exist beyond making the world feel authentic and the possibility that something of value could be snaffled away inside.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Shops, bars and clubs are lovingly detailed, and once inside you're free to toy with the world. Buy something, drink something for a stat bonus, steal something, change your clothes, or earwig and people watch. Sometimes you'll need to change outfits, because it throws off the cops chasing you; sometimes just because you feel you should wear beach clothes on the beach, because I'm completely hooked into this world.

The geography is considered too. Vice City is a maze of overpasses and winding spaghetti motorway junctions; the city itself is a muddle of back alleys, malls, and beachfront hotels, while the roads out in the country are simpler and more relaxed; the swamps need care to navigate; the sandy, wooded isles of the north are a stolen boat. Beaches, swamps, forests and distinct neighbourhoods all have their own character, and you feel it: stressed in Vice City, calm and playful up north, the mullet of map design, if you will. Even the residents and police behave differently depending on where you are.

Early on, Jason and Lucia visit a rich, enclaved community filled with jewellery shops, polished pavements and high-fashion stores practically demanding to be robbed. A policeman on a bicycle stops them and warns them that their kind isn't welcome. I pushed my luck, choosing confrontational dialogue options, refused to obey, and he called in backup from other pedal-bike cops who made it clear our kind wasn't welcome. I returned at night and stole everything, and it felt so good.

Giving you an emotional reason to do things is one of GTA VI's biggest successes. You start to understand the people who live here, the divisions between communities and the little injustices that make you want to cause trouble.

There's always something happening, too. An armoured car is robbed, so I follow it to the thieves' hideout and steal everything. A farm sign says 'pilot wanted', so I drop in and end up in a whole side story about meth-strawberries that eventually riffs on a Marvel character I never expected. Leonida's residents are 'Karens on crack', too. Scrape someone's car, and they'll chase you down; look at someone too long, and they'll demand a fight; drive down a motorway, and hyped up teen will lean out of their car to challenge you to a race. Once I planned a bank heist, only to find a random gang shooting the place up, and I got caught in the melee. It's layer upon layer of random, living events, and even on a mission, it's easy to get sidetracked as gunshots ring out.

GTA VI rewards your downtime too; it wants you to simply enjoy the place and the moment because conversations eavesdropped on in a bar are hilarious but also tease secrets about the world, whether residents are complaining about the weather or arguing over culture-war nonsense raised by the State's shock jock, who is furious about that weekend's Manatees football result and the demise of 'mansculinity'. Some can be engaged with and will share random but useful news about Leonida.

There's no Ubisoft-style checklist here. Stunts, hidden collectable cards (which you can sell in-game), fishing challenges and sporting events are there if you want them, but the world grows as you explore, meet people and build up your contacts list. You just exist in Leonida and enjoy exploring, competing and completing things.

The weather is a big part of that experience, because it looks beautiful – golden morning sunlight cuts through thick mist over a wildflower meadow with realism, dramatic storm clouds and dense golden fog engulf a city skyline, obscuring buildings and bridges in an atmospheric haze.

But weather also affects how you engage with the world. Days feel long enough to play in, different things happen at different times, and the weather is dramatic and distinct. That hazy mist can obscure your visibility, while hard rain can limit distance and disrupt sound, something used to dramatic effect in a nighttime kidnapping rescue where large halogen lights pierced the rain and mist, creating drama but affecting line of sight in some spaces.

Likewise, a plane handles differently in wind, rain and cloud, as the controls judder and inputs feel less responsive. Flying through a storm, with lightning sparking and rolling across the horizon, gives you a real sense of place and moment but also puts you slightly on edge.

Jason and Lucia's relationship really surprised me in GTA VI, and it's one area where Rockstar picks up where Red Dead Redemption 2 left off. Both are well-rounded protagonists with motivations and shared dreams that you help build. Lucia is alive and sprightly, Jason is dour and determined, and how their connection develops, or doesn't, becomes a game of its own.

A subtle romance and empathy system is at play. How much time the pair spend together, the conversations you choose, the dates, time at home (yes, you can make love in the shower, on the sofa, in the kitchen and, well, all sorts of places) and even how and when you plan and commit crimes all feed into how their relationship develops, and it can affect how their story ends.

What you do on a job matters too. Kill lots of people, and you get a different criminal rating than if you spare lives, and the duo seem to have a healthier relationship if you play to control a room with threats or shoot to injure rather than murder. I wanted a loving crime couple, so almost without meaning to, I started shooting people in the legs and arms to make them fall or drop their guns instead of headshotting everyone in a room. I wanted my Lucia to like my Jason.

Likewise, when Jason went undercover as 'the poolboy' for a saucy film shoot, I held back on how far I took things. Lucia was getting madder in my ear as Jason applied lotion to an actress, and when given the choice to go all in, as it were, I pulled out, as they say, as it were, because I wanted Lucia to still like Jason. I still don't know how far you can take that mission, but this is Rockstar, so I imagine it's all the way (and that's what she said).

Few games get that emotional connection right. It doesn't come only from good writing and characterisation, but from all the little conversations, actions, reactions and animated moments when they meet up or succeed. You'd have a heart of stone to go out of your way to ruin their romance, because you can. You monster.

Controlling when and how they meet up is part of GTA V's character-switching development. Moving between them is nearly instantaneous: the camera pulls out to a global view, zooms back down, and you can message the other to hook up or tell them to meet you somewhere. And you do get committed: when I occasionally Irish-goodbye'd Jason, I felt the need to call him and check up.

The central narrative picks up what worked in Red Dead Redemption 2, splitting the story into chapters that each introduce a new gang or cast and a grand setup to plan towards. The structure gives you plenty to play with, and the story spans more years as the couple bounces from backwater crimes to epic, militarised heists. These feed into cinematic tentpole moments that draw on everything from the later Fast and Furious movies to Assault on Precinct 13, with even a little nod to Die Hard as Lucia sparks a lighter in an air vent, laughs and paraphrases the classic line, "Come out to the coast, we'll get together, have a few laughs."

It's also where Rockstar's love of a good heist movie really shines. Some of the bigger set pieces have the clockwork precision of an Edgar Wright film, with different characters, objectives and moving parts all working towards one carefully choreographed finale. The editing is part of the fun: the action cuts between Jason and Lucia as they tackle their separate jobs, each sequence dovetailing with the next as the plan unfolds, the clock ticks down, and the stakes rise.

The grand finales of each chapter are proper spectacles that never play out the same way and deliver 'cinema'. You might be flying gunships over a stormy ocean, or swapping between Jason and Lucia as they complete different parts of a larger plan. Jason races to a rooftop to stop mobster reinforcements while Lucia hacks a vault, and you're jumping between the two as the action cuts back and forth, the tempo building with each switch. One moment you're holding off a gang; the next, you're working through the other side of the operation, and it all clicks together like clockwork. It's a wonderfully cinematic way to make character switching part of the action, not just a convenient way to get around the map.

Around these set pieces that take time to build are lower-key missions, some tailored to each character, and this is where Rockstar earns its rewards. The satire of modern America, social media, celebrity culture and consumerism that we love about GTA is here in abundance. A favourite is a storyline in which Lucia becomes embroiled in a bored-housewives vape cult that's like Goop meets Elizabeth Holmes.

Then there are the random encounters that make Leonida feel active, and never run how you think. An elderly woman screaming for help on a back road took me to her farmhouse, where I expected a robbery or a rescue. Instead, a client had 'died' in a bondage orgy gone wrong, and I needed to dispose of the body in a river. Even that didn't end as I expected.

Even 40-plus hours into the main story, Rockstar finds new ways to surprise me. It introduces a vault-hacking mini-game that uses haptics and controller prompts for one bank job, then drops in a drug-dog sidekick for a single mission. Ideas are picked up, enjoyed and dropped before they go stale. GTA VI has so many that it never has to hang around with one for long.

Shooting and weapon handling are superb, and each gun feels distinct. The cover system and enemy AI respond nicely even in busy rooms, and stealth is reliable and effective. While the big set-piece story missions can feel a little restrictive and scripted because they need to reach the cinematic heights Rockstar is aiming for, anything can happen outside them.

A bank heist, for example, needs proper planning. Park a getaway car, choose the right vehicle, pick the rear door lock, hack the cameras, wear a disguise, and don't overstay your welcome. The world is so well designed and systematised that everything feels connected. Next time, go in through the front door, or steal a truck and pull an ATM from the wall. Heists in backwater towns are easier because there are fewer police around. And nothing plays out quite as you expect; every bank is unique, and after two seamless jobs I go for a third and it all goes wrong – an unexpected teller wanders into the office for a coffee, an alarm is tripped, and before I realise it, I'm shooting my way out, bags shouldered, and looking for a new car to steal… the best-laid plans are shot.

The police react to all this more deeply than in previous GTAs. There's no longer just a star rating and a zone to escape, but how you escape matters. Swap cars and clothes, and they'll lose you, because they're looking for your description, not you, me, the player. All the old tricks are still here, from roadblocks and air support to increasingly aggressive police AI, but you have new ways to shake them off beyond just driving fast.

It ties into car ownership too, another Red Dead Redemption 2 influence. You can't carry everything, so it's worth stowing a change of clothes and weapons in your car. Carrying a gun openly gets the police involved, but some Vice City passers-by will also decide to take you out as well.

Driving feels familiar from GTA V, but with enough nuance to feel like an evolution, as cars have different weights and handling, and each one reacts differently through the DualSense triggers: sports cars resist less than family saloons when you pull to accelerate. Boats, bikes, planes and helicopters all work as you'd expect, but even here there are subtle shifts in how responsive each can be – one helicopter I stole was uncontrollable and spun into the swamp.

Character models, facial animation, skin, hair, and clothing all deliver the hyperrealism I expected from a new GTA, though they're still larger-than-life caricatures built to feel relatable rather than photorealistic.

Animation, including the transitions between gameplay and cutscenes, is where GTA VI takes its biggest strides. Lucia and Jason are wonderfully handled, whether it's the little snuggles and embraces or the way they hold up a bank and play off one another, but the breadth of animation across GTA VI is what impresses. Every Leonida resident feels uniquely animated, and it's fun just to people-watch. Early on, a drunk girl follows Jason around a bar and is authentically annoying, and the nightlife feels realistically overwhelming. Bar bands are animated to sell their next song, and even the wildlife has moments: I watched a white-tailed doe and buck nuzzle each other lovingly and naturally through Jason's rifle scope. It was cute enough to make me take a breath, but Jason needs more money, so the shot rang out and the wildlife scattered.

Leonida has a recognisable visual identity, bold and vibrant, with every corner full of quirks, from the deep forests of the north to the out-of-town mall and rows of copy-and-paste suburban houses. Fictional adverts, billboards, shops, signage, and TV build the world, as if you see an ad for a beer or car, and you can buy it (or steal it). Beyond signage, graffiti walls, sculptures, exhibits, and more invite you to linger and just take in the world.

It also feels like a realistic evolution of the 1980s Vice City I knew and loved, a city with a history inside a broader world, with references to Liberty City aplenty, from car number plates to Jason and Lucia's accents. It's somewhere to wallow, whether you're having a cocktail under palm trees swaying in a breeze or tearing up Vice City in a neon-lit supercar while crypto bros trade and wannabe rappers parade.

It's a wonder this all runs on a base PS5. I remember the mess of equally ambitious games like Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, but GTA VI is in a different league. The frame rate is locked at 30fps, and it's fine: stable, with little slowdown or stutter, and controls and handling feel spot on. There's occasional soft pop-in, but few visual compromises or trip-ups. You can feel the work that's gone into making everything run smoothly, and GTA 6 is polished to perfection.

I'm really only scratching the surface. Familiar street races, bank heists, and chilled fishing and hunting trips are joined by crypto rug pulls, golf tournaments, and deep-sea treasure hunts. Or I just drive, hunt a swamp thing, stop to solve a mystery from a local ad, or relax with a game of pool and a Patriot beer. You can take on the State's sports and races, go sailing, or listen to 80s FM hits, the biggest dance tracks, or to the MAGA-inspired Richard Bastion Show – "more volume than logic" – who's mad about everything.

This game has video games inside it that feel more complete than some real games I've played, from the top-down sci-fi shooter Time Jackers: Rewind to a lightgun score-chasing bar game Bang For Your Buck. And in typical Rockstar fashion, they all have a satirical edge, like the indie auteur game Tenebrae Lux, which pokes fun at the po-faced walking sims that were all the rage: it's black-and-white, minimal, and filled with overwritten prose like a Taylor Swift song about metaphors.

GTA VI is a world that exists beyond its main story, where everything feeds into and off each other. It's the best world-building I've experienced in a game in years, partly because its systems all work in a coherent, purposeful and layered way, but also because it's not afraid to be weird, whether that's discovering the dumpster lawyer, becoming a frog, slobbing on the sofa and watching an episode of Whose Dick's Whose, or finding an influencer in the boot of a stolen car who wants to be kidnapped for clout.

There are minor restrictions, mainly when the big cinematic missions take over and funnel you down a more scripted path, but for good reason, and the 30fps cap won't suit everyone (yet it's really not an issue). But in a game that otherwise gives you this much freedom, they're the exception.

13 years? The wait has been worthwhile. I still set off with a plan, get distracted by something ridiculous at the side of the road, and lose another hour to a game I thought I'd finished. I laughed within minutes of starting, and I laugh every time I play. I've also been stressed, revolted, astonished, baffled, heartbroken and euphoric. I've run the full gamut of emotions, and I still do each time I return to Vice City.

#9167. Native Artist Receives $10K Grant to Revive Visor Craftmaking

Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) will use the Walker Youngbird Foundation grant to revive the qayaatx̂ux, or chief visor.

The Walker Youngbird Foundation named Native artist Dustin Newman (Unangax̂/Deg Hit’an Athabascan) the annual recipient of its Núhi grant today, November 19. The Alaskan artist will use the $10,000 award to revive and pass down the endangered craftsmanship behind qayaatx̂ux, traditional closed crown visors worn by Unangax̂ chiefs.

Through technical research with the Anchorage Museum and collaborations with regional hat-makers, Newman will produce a small series of visors to gift to cultural leaders. An intricately decorated hunting hat historically worn by chiefs and high-ranking whaling captains, the qayaatx̂ux began fading into obscurity in the early 20th century due to factors including American colonization. After completing the series, Newman will share the tradition with community members through Camp Qungaayux on the island of Unalaska and the Agdaagux Culture Camp in King Cove, the fishing village where the artist was raised.

"I first started bending visors at 17 with my mentor Okalena Patricia Lekanoff-Gregory at our regional culture camp in Anchorage and Unalaska," Newman told Hyperallergic. "Why I chose to pursue this project through the Núhi Grant was to uplift the status of these visors not as a wall hanging but as a symbol within our communities honoring our culture bearers and community leaders."

#9166. Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” said the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges said. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

“The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

“Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic company, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”

Looking ahead, the judges said “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

“Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

“This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges said. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

“This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

“As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”

#9165. Iraq’s national museum announces reopening after major renovations

The Iraq Museum in Baghdad has been closed for two years for renovations Photo: Hussein A.Al-Mukhtar via Wikimedia

The Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several new galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Several important artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The new Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the new government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are plans afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

According to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while new ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has announced that a new museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Al-Dakhili has also announced that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement says.

#9164. Art Dealer Sentenced for Falsely Claiming Native Heritage

Jose Martinez adopted the name Joseph Skywolf and ran a traveling gallery that sold products falsely marketed as Native, violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act.

This month, a Las Vegas man pled guilty to a felony violation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 after being charged with selling counterfeit Native American art misrepresented as authentic to consumers. A United States district court judge for Nevada sentenced Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf, to two years of supervised probation and court-ordered restitution for the infraction.

A release from the US Department of the Interior's Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) outlined that Martinez falsely claimed to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American while promoting his mobile business Skywolf's Gallery. Through the business, which was once headquartered in Jackson, Wyoming, but traveled to venues and markets across the Great Plains and Southwest, Martinez deliberately sold counterfeit artwork and handicrafts, including headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides falsely attributed to Native artists or specific tribes.

Last summer, Martinez was indicted on one count of violating the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, which prohibits the sale of products falsely marketed as authentic American Indian or Alaska Native art and craftwork. The act is intended to protect the livelihoods, cultural knowledge, and artistic traditions of recognized Native tribes, bands, and communities, as well as consumers seeking authentic cultural heritage and art objects.

#9163. Logitech MX Keypad review: Can nine LCD keys take the pain out of Photoshop?

A smart, compact control surface with real potential, the Logitech MX Keypad has plenty of presets and context-aware functions for the best software and utilities, but you’ll only get your money’s worth if you put in the setup time.

Options+ is context-aware and offers presets for popular apps

LCD keys show a changing icon for each function

15 'pages' of custom keys is a ludicrous amount

A good alternative to native drawing tablet remotes

It’s wired only, which is disappointing at this price

Unsupported apps such as Rebelle and ArtRage need manual setup

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Connection: Wired USB-C, 1.5m USB-C to USB-C

Features: Logi Options+, app-specific, automatically switching

Supported apps: Adobe Creative Cloud, Figma, Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, VS Code, IntelliJ, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Zoom, Slack, Google (beta), and more

I’m always drawn to gadgets that promise to save time or make things easier and more accessible, whether it's the best drawing tablets, shortcut keyboards, or odd little controllers parked next to my mouse: if it claims to shave seconds off a repetitive job, I want to try it. Photoshop is my worst offender, because half the battle is remembering where Adobe has hidden things this time with each new update.

The Logitech MX Keypad is a desktop control pad with nine customisable LCD keys, each showing an icon for whatever you’ve assigned to it. Two physical buttons flip between pages, so you get more shortcuts without another huge peripheral crowding your desk. It's in the Logitech MX line, gadgets aimed as much at creatives as at everyday folk looking to make life easier.

At $99.99 / £89.99, it’s not an impulse buy but something you should consider, and after years of drilling Ctrl, Alt and Shift combos into my left hand, I wasn’t sure I needed one. I also use a drawing tablet and stylus for art, so I have just enough buttons on the pen, or I can access more on my tablet's virtual keyboard. But knowing a shortcut and having a button for the thing you hit countless times an hour, whether it's in Photoshop, calling up Google files or browser pages, is a different matter. That's where the MX keypad aims to be a decent all-rounder for everyday work and creative projects alike.

Nine square keys sit in a three-by-three grid, and because each has its own screen, the icons change based on what you’ve assigned. That beats a traditional macro pad with fixed labels: you can see what a button does instead of memorising obscure combos.

It works with the best digital art software and creative apps, including Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom, Premiere Pro, and Figma. Importantly, it’s context-aware, so you can select your app in Logitech Options+ and it loads presets for that software’s most common tools; from there, you can edit or set up your own actions.

Nine keys run out fast, so using up to 15 'pages' of nine preset buttons (135 total assigned actions) earns it keep as a feature. Overkill, yes, but some will want all that power at a button press. The Options+ app lets you build separate layouts for different jobs, one for Photoshop, another for Lightroom and so on. Rather than living with Adobe’s shortcuts, you build the layout around how you work, and it's as easy as going into the Options+ app and assigning keyboard shortcuts to the buttons, including combinations of buttons, and it supports different saved shortcut collections, so you can also tailor favourites to different apps.

At roughly 92 x 78 x 25mm, it sits beside a mouse and keyboard without taking over, and it's easy to hold, which matters if your desk already hosts a pen tablet or display. A kickstand and a 1.5m USB-C cable come in the box.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

It’s not perfect. The keys lack the click of good mechanical keys, but they do have an old-fashioned soft-push feel, much like an old 90s dial-up digital phone, but that also means you need a little force to push one, and the stand lacks weight or 'stick', so it drifts as you press. The solution? Hold it by the top and depress with my thumb. I do like how each button has its own little digital decal icon showing its function, and you can buy sticky pads to keep it in place.

It’s also wired only, which is a little surprising at this price, but it's not the end of the world, and the cable is long enough for most setups.

For me, the MX Keypad makes the most sense with Photoshop (I've also downloaded and set it up for Clip Studio Paint, CorelDRAW, Google, and Slack), and even fast keyboard users end up wishing something were easier to reach. Favourite brushes, colour swapping and new layers all suit the MX Keypad, and you can split them across pages for selections, masking, painting, and layer management. I’m a light Photoshop user, but I found that adding shortcuts for Lasso selections, favourite brushes, and layer options sped up how I use the software.

When I’m drawing, I don’t want to look down at the keyboard or lift my hand off the tablet, so a few key actions right beside my drawing area help. For the most part, I find the custom buttons on a stylus work well alongside touch controls on a tablet, but if you are more professionally minded and need all the options all the time, a shortcut keypad is essential. While XPPen, Huion, and Xencelabs all offer good remotes, the MX Keypad is a step above, with more buttons, more configuration options, and easy-to-understand icons and button labels.

If you’re already quick on a keyboard, reaching across to press a button may not be any faster. The gain is in the visual reminders and having rarely used commands grouped on pages somewhere easy to find. With only nine keys, you’ll need to plan your pages carefully, but for serious users, once organised, you'll be able to cycle to function collections at speed.

Of course, not all apps are supported; for example, Rebelle and ArtRage aren’t here, but you can add the apps manually and set up profiles and shortcuts based on keyboard commands; it just takes more time than Logitech’s preset app library. Using presets is as simple as clicking a drop-down menu, but adding and editing a new app setup and customising each key can take around 30 minutes per 'page'.

Because profiles are set per app, the buttons change colour and icon designs as you switch software. I found this to be the MX Keypad's strength, because it becomes one device that can follow you around your creative workflow, so if you’re someone who works between software, from Blender to Photoshop, for example, the MX Keypad can follow along.

Options+, the same app used by the MX Master 4 Special Edition mouse, can configure everything, but it takes some time to get used to if you’re editing a new app that isn’t supported out of the box. If you use the most popular, most common software, it’s easy; if you use niche apps, it can feel far from plug-and-play, since you have to manually enter each keyboard command.

For artists and designers who bounce between the biggest and most common apps, it’s a compact way to build your own control pad, and LCD keys beat cryptic labels on a standard macro pad or half-remembered keyboard shortcuts.

At $99.99 / £89.99, the Logitech MX Keypad is a fair price for a quick key remote. By comparison, the Xencelabs Quick Keys cost a similar $99.99 / £95.90 and also have LCD icons, but only words and no images, while the decent XPPen Remote is $49.99 / £49.99 but more basic than both Xencelabs and the Logitech. Both are wireless remotes, unlike the MX Keypad, but as a shortcut remote, the MX Keypad is the best of the three because Options+ offers an easy setup with established software and a huge number of buttons and pages.

But the MX Keypad has more going for it than those remotes: more custom buttons, more context-aware presets, and the option to use ‘pages’, which packs a staggering number of functions onto one face. The big advantage over a traditional drawing tablet remote is two-fold: you get little icons that explain each function, plus the depth of Options+ with multiple pre-loaded shortcuts for the best graphic design software and art apps out of the box.

Do beginners and hobbyists like me need this much choice? I mostly use two to three apps, for example, and three or four functions, and I don't need speed, but if you're a pro with a library of art, design, 3D, and video editing software to pair with and move across in one project, it would be a good gadget. For pros and tinkerers, it’s essential; for everyone else, it may be overkill.

#9162. Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture

In her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist.

Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm.

Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.

The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

#9161. The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo

Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.

ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Detail of Carolina Caycedo, "Neodymium Intensive" (2026), colored pencil, aluminum and variegated metal leaf on paper (left); Installation view of "Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star" (2023) at Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots at the Kemper Art Museum

Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

It's astonishing that, for many creatives, the office chair is often the last thing that's thought about when working from home. I personally know creative professionals that only bought a dedicated ergonomic office chair for their home office several years after the 2020 WFH revolution.

For the last six years I've made it my mission to test and review the best office chairs for back pain, so that when great retail events come around, like Black Friday, I'm in a good position to find the best deals on the best chairs.

That's exactly what I've done below – finding the best crop of early Black Friday office chair deals from the best brands.

When it comes to price, comfort, adjustability and value, this is the king of chairs. Sure, I've had better looking, more flash chairs. But for $169, nothing touches the Sihoo M18 – and no other company seems to try! At $139 this is a strong recommendation (especially if you can get it in one of the groovy colours).

The best mid-priced chair I've reviewed. It's comfy and has lots of adjustability, including a padded, two-way adjustable lumbar support for back health. I also like the classy understated aesthetic. A $50 discount might not seem like a lot, but this was already the best-value ergonomic chair on the market.

See my full five-star Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro review.

The Capisco is my own favourite office chair, because the unusual saddle seat style encourages me to keep shifting between sitting, perching and standing. It's firmer than a conventional chair, but it's ideal if you use a standing desk, and it looks like quirkily stylish too.

Autonomous make some of the best ergo chairs out there, and this is their best-priced chair for the amount of adjustments you get. So I absolutely love the $30 off. Highly recommend.

This unusual office chair could appeal if you want cloud-like comfort over deep ergonomic customisability. It has a hybrid cushion combining plush foam with nested coils, making it feel more like a cozy lounge chair than a stiff mesh or industrial task chair. The plush design allows it to blend more easily into a home office or hybrid space without giving an office furniture look.

Branch’s Multitask chair is the one of the US-based furniture manufacturer’s cheapest offerings, and it strips everything to the fundamentals. There's no lumbar support, but it has a solid build and premium feel for a very reasonable price.

See our full Branch Multitask chair review.

Our reviewer rated this a perfect 10 out of 10, and for good reason. Its 14 points of adjustment, 5D armrests and thick, soft seat are wrapped in a chic design that will lift any home office. Even at full price, it's the best mid-range ergonomic chair we've tested.

With its sculpted lines and bold colour options, the Verve is one of the best-looking office chairs around. Our reviewer found it comfortable for long work sessions, with excellent lumbar support and a nicely balanced recline.

Our reviewer gave the M18 a rare five stars, calling it the new gold standard for budget ergonomic chairs. Its wide W-shaped seat, breathable mesh back and excellent headrest make it comfortable for long sessions, and it looks far smarter than its price suggests.

With 3D armrests, an adjustable headrest and a cushioned lumbar support that our reviewer called the star of the show, the M57 does ergonomics well for the money. It's mesh throughout, so it keeps you cool, though very tall users may find it a bit of a squeeze.

Our reviewer found the Steelcase Gesture comfortable and superbly built, with some of the best armrests he's ever tested. Assembly takes minutes, it's made in France and it comes with a generous 12-year warranty.

So which should you choose? In the US, the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro offers the best balance of comfort, adjustability and looks we've found, while the Branch Verve is the one for design lovers. The Hinomi H2 Pro is ideal if you're tall or love tweaking every detail. And if you're happy to rethink how you work altogether, the HAG Capisco remains in a class of its own.

In the UK, the Sihoo M18 is the easy pick if you're on a budget: it's comfortable, stylish and remarkably well designed for the price, though it arrives in a lot of pieces. The Sihoo M57 is a solid option if you want 3D armrests and an all-mesh design, while the Steelcase Gesture is a premium chair built to last for years.

Whichever you go for, check the height range before you buy, as even the best chair won't help if it doesn't fit your body. And remember, Prime Day deals will only last for a few more hours!

#9159. Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M

The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.

Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

#9158. Artists should receive tax breaks for donating their own work to UK museums, says new philanthropy report

The National Gallery's Project Domani is cited as a success story that shows “what focused giving can achieve” for UK institutions

Artists who donate their own works to museums and galleries in the UK should receive tax breaks according to a new report published on Wednesday (18 November) focused on boosting cultural philanthropy.

The idea is one of a number of “tax enabling” proposals put forward by the think tank, The Cultural Policy Unit (CPU), which stresses in the report, “A National Strategy for Cultural Philanthropy”, that philanthropy “should be treated as both an urgent [UK] strategic priority and a deliberate instrument of cultural policy”.

The funding environment for culture has changed fundamentally, argues CPU which adds that “public finances have tightened considerably over the last 15 years, government funding for the arts has declined and self-generated income, while a key area, has not succeeded in plugging the widening gap.”

In a wide-ranging set of recommendations, the report also suggests establishing a King’s Philanthropy Medal for Culture and setting up a national cultural “match-and-seed funding” programme with a regional focus.

Alison Cole, the director of the CPU and former editor of The Art Newspaper, says: “While the arts funding environment has changed dramatically in recent years, the philanthropic landscape has hardly kept pace let alone filled the gap with the UK lagging far behind the incentives offered by many of our European and US counterparts. We need a new national strategy that not only identifies the opportunities and need, but also thrives on a spirit of creative collaboration and mutual respect.”

Artists who donate their own works to qualifying cultural institutions should receive tax recognition based on independent valuation, says the think tank. Other tax-based recommendations include protecting charitable giving through inheritance planning—which means simplifying inheritance tax rules—and providing clearer rules around VAT.

Charles Saumarez Smith, who previously led the National Gallery, National Portrait Gallery and the Royal Academy of Arts, told The Art Newspaper that the report is “sensible”. “I particularly appreciated the information as to how other countries encourage philanthropy, not just the US,” he says. “The biggest issue seems to me to be the lack of clarity round the existing systems, including, for example, around inheritance. How many people, even within cultural institutions, knows how this operates?”

The CPU acknowledges that Britain has a strong philanthropic tradition, arguing that its potential for cultural giving remains unrealised. Gift Aid, Acceptance in Lieu and the Cultural Gifts Scheme have all delivered real benefits but these schemes should be enhanced so that donors are more aware of their benefits, the report says.

UK incentives are “broadly generous, but they are structured very differently from overseas models,“ according to the report. “The practical result is that British donors give quietly and anonymously, while the US and other systems reward public foundations and naming opportunities.”

Kate Rolfe, a cultural strategy consultant, says: "Art organisations need to work with philanthropists who are inspired by the organisational vision and share their values and priorities, ensuring that the museum can stay focused on its purpose, vision and audiences." She believes corporate donations need to be reincentivised, as these often "lead to really creative partnerships based on shared audiences and values". Rolfe founded The Revels Office, a strategic audience and commercial development consultancy for the culture sector.

“Focused giving” may be partly the answer says the CPU, as evidenced by the Domani project at the National Gallery in London with £375m secured from Crankstart, the charitable foundation of Sir Michael Moritz and his wife Harriet Heyman, and the Julia Rausing Trust for a new Modern art wing. “The real transformation needs to be across the country and not just in the capital,” adds Cole.

#9157. Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year announced

An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.

The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau. It was also named residential interior (small) project of the year.

“This was probably the boldest and most well-executed project we saw,” said the judges.

“They kept everything that was already there and made a much more interesting place,” adding that, “it’s very well-thought-out in terms of how space has been used.”

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects

The winning project of the year was up against category winners, including a restaurant that features “direct and unrefined” materials to create tactile interior in Canada, a pink stepped-facade-fronted commercial building and interiors in Mexico and a boutique that recalls a traditional yurt in Kazakhstan.

A boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture and a warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning interiors projects below:

Interiors project of the year and residential interior (small) of the year: La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects

The Spanish practice renovated the home in Mataro, Spain, which belonged to a sailor in the 19th century, updating its interiors to suit the lifestyle of his descendant, who lives there now.

There was no discussion – this was the winner

The project saw the renovation of three spaces: the entrance hall, the dining room and the living area. The judges praised the project’s bold approach, noting there was no deliberation over its winning credentials: “There was no discussion – this was the winner.”

“It’s super unusual,” they continued, “and we liked to see an intervention in a very historical space where they decided to not play it safe.”

Residential interior (large) of the year: Garden Home by Gisbert Pöppler

Local studio Gisbert Pöppler won residential interior (large) of the year for its renovation of a 1920s villa in Ruhr, Germany.

For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior

The interior design features a bold colour scheme and artisanal details that reflect its association with the Deutscher Werkbund movement, which caught the judges’ eyes.

“For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior,” they said.

“It has character and doesn’t play it safe,” they continued.

Restaurant interior of the year: Jeju by &Daughters

Canadian studio &Daughters won restaurant interior of the year for Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver, Canada.

This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element

A rich material palette of basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood characterises the restaurant interior, which nods to traditional touches in its contemporary design.

“This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element,” the master jury said. “It’s contemporary and still a bit traditional. There’s also a cultural influence that’s being used well and isn’t just there for decoration.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Bar and cafe interior of the year: Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design

Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design in Xi’an, China, won bar and cafe interior of the year, sponsored by Programa.

There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it

Located inside the Beilin Museum, the cafe’s interior aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty and used a minimal intervention renovation strategy with every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

“This project is new and modern, but still connected to the past,” the judges said.

“There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.”

“The architect has taken symbolic elements and simplified them, which makes it feel quite fresh.”

Hotel and short-stay interior of the year: Moon Gang by YSG Studio

Australian studio YSG won hotel and short-stay interior of the year for its conversion of a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali, Indonesia.

There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit

Focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture, Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

YSG was influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit,” commended the master jury.

Workplace interior (small) of the year: Rosadoce by Reims 502

Rosadoce by Reims 502 in Querétaro, Mexico won workplace interior (small) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior

Featuring a stepped facade, the commercial building’s pink characterises the warm feel of the interior, being used throughout the workplace with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone.

“This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior,” noted the master jury.

“We like how they connected the interior and exterior design,” they continued, “it’s an adaptable and very sophisticated design.”

Workplace interior (large) of the year: Not A Hotel Office by Not A Hotel

Not a Hotel’s own office in Tokyo, Japan won workplace interior (large) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic

The Japanese hospitality company’s in-house architecture team turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace featuring a brutalist design divided by glass partitions and a spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

“We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic,” said the judges.

“It really makes coming to the office feel like a dip back into the culture.”

Retail interior (small) of the year: Gunia Project Showroom by Temp Project

Local studio Temp Project won retail interior (small) of the year for its lifestyle store in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The mix between the old and new is very interesting

Modern materials, including mirrors and tiled surfaces, were used to complement the building’s original ornate interior for brand Gunia Project, which occupies the ground floor of a late 19th-century building located on a historic street near Kyiv’s Golden Gate.

“The mix between the old and new is very interesting,” said the judges.

“It must have been a constraining space to work in,” they observed, “but the end result feels very carefully edited and sophisticated.”

Retail interior (large) of the year: Messa House by Up2date

Up2date Architects won retail interior (large) of the year for the minimalist Messa House store in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect

Commissioned for womenswear brand Messa, the 350-square-metre store was designed to reimagine the form of a Kazakh yurt, with breakout areas and an on-site cafe.

“Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect,” praised the master jury.

The judges also commended “the contrast between the glossy tiles, wall and furniture”.

“It’s like a small architectural world inside the space,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Leisure and wellness interior of the year: Unravel by Atelier Write

Japanese studio Atelier Write won the leisure and wellness interior of the year for its hair salon project in Tokyo, Japan.

This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there

Named Unravel, the project transformed a warehouse with statement features such as suspending mirrors, shelves and curtains from a series of industrial rails that allow the entire space to be reconfigured.

“This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there,” said the judges.

“It’s an innovative, moveable space and the movement has purpose; it’s not just a gimmick.”

Exhibition design (interior) of the year: Life Behind the Walls by B² Architecture

B2 Architecture won exhibition design (interior) of the year for its Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, Czech Republic.

They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way

Using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea, the 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

“In this project, the colours black, white and red are used really well in a graphical way,” said the master jury.

The judges also noted its material sensitivity, noting how surprising “the designers use soft materials to create emotions,” adding that “there’s a contrast between the technology and the use of textiles”.

“They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way,” they added.

Kitchen interior of the year: Pine Island Cottage by Thom Fougere Studio & Bureau Tempo

Canadian studios Bureau Tempo and Thom Fougere won kitchen interior of the year for Pine Island Cottage in Ontario, Canada.

You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them

The getaway retreat’s materials are informed by the rocky surroundings of the host island in Ontario’s Georgian Bay.

“This kitchen is very functional and well laid out, but it’s also super beautiful and we like that they used local materials,” said the master jury.

“You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.”

Bathroom interior of the year: Lumeah by Pepper & Well

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well won bathroom interior of the year for Lumeah in Macedon, Australia.

We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass

The studio took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing the new en-suite within one of the most intact examples of residential work by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

“We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass,” said the judges.

“The studio did a good job of creating a contemporary interior in a historic building, and we enjoyed how the bathroom feels like it continues out into the garden.”

Sustainable interior of the year: Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo Design Studio

Chinese studio RooMoo won sustainable interior of the year for Cloudhaus Hotel in Chongqing, China.

This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins were repurposed for the 24-room retreat for its renovation, which the judges noted for being well-documented.

“This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done,” the master jury said.

“They took a dark, concrete space and turned it into a warm interior through the use of wood, while keeping a lot of the existing materials,” they continued.
