Dundee studio Bit Loom’s Glenmara: Still Life Artist ditches scoring and failure to capture the cosy spirit of small island communities.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're looking for an antidote to the GTA 6 noise, Glenmara: Still Life Artist is it. Think of still life art, and chances are an oil painting of fruit in a bowl or flowers in a vase. While you may be presented with those options in Glenmara, this casual, cosy game from four-person Dundee-based indie studio Bit Loom Games also lets you get creatively weird with more contemporary objects and styles.

Despite the title, it's also not a painting game like, say, Mario Paint, but rather a simulation. "It's just this small idea based on being interested in how scenes are composed," artist Caitlin Smith tells me.

Instead, it's about being given objects you can assemble and position, then choosing filters and styles with the available tools and letting the game render it for you. Artist Douglas Flinders adds, "The thinking there is you are playing the role of a competent artist, so the player has access to nice painting styles. It's like you don't need to be able to triple-jump in real life to do it in Mario. You get to feel that fantasy without necessarily needing the inherent skill yourself."

Even though you are technically painting on a canvas, the filters you have available aren't limited to painting styles. Sure, you can use traditional oil paints or watercolours, but you can also opt for mosaic or styles that resemble cel-shading or pixel art. Being free to break from conventional expectations has been an important design decision.

"The [initial] idea was that you could be scored on how well you compose a theme with traditional rules, but it changed pretty quickly after we realised it would just be much more fun to not have any rules and basically be able to do whatever you want creatively," Smith explains. "It was important to us to not have any sort of failed state. So if you want to sort of make this niche for yourself as a painter that puts eggs in all of your paintings, the game is not going to tell you you can't do that."

As the team's first game made with the open-source engine Godot, which only launched its own asset store earlier this year, all of Glenmara's shaders for its different art styles were created from scratch by programmer Henry Pullan.

"Coming to Godot from Unity, the image processing pipeline we were used to just wasn't there, and we had to come up with a different way of getting all the data to and from the GPU at the right time," Pullan explains. "Fortunately, they're not real-time effects, and being able to process the image over a few frames lets us really easily experiment."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

"This led to a system where we can stack effects on top of each other to create pretty different outcomes. The majority of the effects are using the library of shaders we've built up in different combinations to create a variety of effects."

While playing as a newcomer to the fictional Scottish island of Glenmara might have you thinking of the premise of other cosy games like Animal Crossing: New Horizons, the inspiration is closer to home for Bit Loom's members, who all grew up in small places, including one from Jersey in the Channel Islands.

"We're going for the small-knit community part of Scotland where everyone kind of knows each other," says Smith. "We tried to put this in the game in various ways, including character dialects, topics of conversation, your object collection and certain events that feature in the narrative. We hope that all of these things can work together to create a comforting, homely feel for players, and even a nostalgic one for some."

This also means avoiding the trap of turning the game into a cosy capitalist sim where your still-life art is your side hustle, and you're incentivised to earn money from commissions to unlock more content.

"It would restrict creativity, and we just want people to go crazy and do loads of cool stuff in a painting," says Flinders. "Also, the story we want to tell and the feeling you get throughout is a lot more about making these pieces of artwork as gifts for members of your community that you're getting to know in a new place you've moved to. You're forming relationships with these people."

Glenmara: Still Life Artist is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#9117. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9116. Ahmed Morsi, Whose Poetic Paintings Long for His Egyptian Homeland, Dies at 96

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

Ahmed Morsi, an Egyptian-born, New York–based painter and poet who once said he had been “displaced most of my life,” died on Wednesday at the age of 96. His death by natural causes in Cairo was confirmed his daughter Sherine Morsi.

In an Instagram post announcing the artist’s death, Sherine wrote, “His profound understanding of our shared humanity, in all its complexity, fragility, and beauty, found expression in both his art and his words.”

Born in Alexandria, Egypt, in 1930, Ahmed Morsi studied drawing in his early years with the Italian artist Silvio Bicchi and became part of the so-called Alexandria School devoted to Surrealist imagery around the time of World War II. But, as he told ARTnews’s Alex Greenberger in 2021, “We need to distinguish between the geographic place that is Egypt’s second largest city from my ‘home.’ My Alexandria is a city of my youth and also myth and legend. This is the ‘home’ that has fueled my imagination, spilling into my poetry notebooks and pouring over my canvas. Don’t look for this Alexandria on your maps.” Related Articles Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Merged Fantasy and Gritty Realism, Dies at 89 Miquel Navarro, Sculptor of Large-Scale, Pared-Down Cities and Valencia's Beloved 'Pink Panther,' Dies at 81

After developing his distinctive painting style—poetic figuration with a quiet sense of fantasy suffused with muted hues—in Egypt and Iraq in the 1950s and ’60s, Morsi moved to New York in 1974 when his wife, Amany Fahmy, got a job as chief of the United Nations Arabic Translation Service. She helped translate some of Morsi’s writing, which took different forms ranging from poetry to art criticism, including the founding of Galerie 68, an influential journal devoted to Arabic modernism based in Cairo.

About his writing, which was as integral as painting to his practice, Morsi once said, “Poetry and painting may be separate media used in a constant attempt to understand the Self, but my vocabulary on paper and on canvas is one.”

In 2021, Morsi featured in MoMA PS1’s survey show “Greater New York,” and, in 2024, his work was part of Adriana Pedrosa’s “Foreigners Everywhere” exhibition for the Venice Biennale. But the world he worked in was his own: As Morsi said in a quote featured on his artist page for his gallery Salon 94, “I am not building a world—for me, that world, my world, exists and has existed since time immemorial. It is a world where everything is seen, perceived and understood differently. Your world is bound by conditioning, preconceived habits. In mine, the senses are free.”

The M4 iPad Air only launched back in March, so a $100 discount could well be the strongest offer we’ll see this Black Friday 2026, and it’s well worth grabbing. It’s the tablet we point most people towards: far cheaper than the Pro, yet it supports Apple Pencil Pro and has plenty of power for digital drawing, photo editing and lighter video work in Final Cut. The newest standard iPad is as good a pick as ever for anyone after an all-rounder for browsing, streaming, casual sketching and note-taking. It also launched back in March 2025, and Amazon knocked $70 off the original price last Black Friday, so this offer could (and I’d argue should) get better.

The newest MacBook Airs arrived in March 2026, and the M5 chip brings a lift in speed for both Apple Intelligence features and creative apps. Thanks to the RAM-driven price rises, they cost more than last year’s model did over Black Friday, so this could be the best offer we see for the rest of 2026.

For the smaller 13in Air, the biggest saving right now is just $70 at Amazon. It was $200 off a couple of days ago, and I’m confident the price will drop again before Black Friday itself.

The M5 Pro MacBook Pros are the ones to buy if you need a machine that won’t struggle with heavy video editing or 3D rendering. #9114. Frieze Abu Dhabi Debuts to Brisk Sales and Confident Dealers

On the morning of Frieze Abu Dhabi’s inaugural edition, Saudi Arabia’s financial center in Riyadh was reportedly attacked by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The crowd in Abu Dhabi, at least, had other things on their minds: the fair was about to open, with millions of dollars’ worth of art ready to be sold. Members of the royal family were back after getting a sneak peek yesterday, alongside politicians and celebrities including tennis star Venus Williams and architect Kulapat Yantrasast.

“It’s about time. Frieze is bringing its A-game to Abu Dhabi, where they have the best museums,” Yantrasast told ARTnews, cheekily mentioning that he’s been putting dots on artworks from The Third Line, Taymour Grahne Projects, Experimenter and Pearl Lam Projects. Related Articles In the Shadow of War, Frieze Abu Dhabi Continues With 'Business as Usual' The Art Market Wanted to Go Global--It Didn't Plan for Everything That Means

The dealers were in high spirits too, as booths started to get busy an hour after the opening. At Thaddeus Ropac, three of Imran Qureshi’s Water Bodies sold for $60,000, each to a UAE-based collection, though the gallery declined to specify whether this was a private or institutional collection.

“There is a great energy around the fair in Abu Dhabi this week. We’re having good conversations with collectors who are well-informed about the artists we are presenting, and you can feel the impact of the institutional scene here,” Xenia Geroulanos, director at Thaddaeus Ropac, told ARTnews.

The fair is under the umbrella of Frieze and has rebranded from Abu Dhabi Art fair, and attendees are noticing a difference. The exhibitor list has been streamlined to 89, down from 142 last year. Dealer Asmaa Al-Shabibi told ARTnews that when she walked through the fair’s new entrance, it felt “a little bit like going into Frieze London, and it feels like a different fair.”

Samy Ghiyati, co-founder of art advisory NG Partners, agreed. “The quality is definitely higher, and galleries made an effort to bring very good inventory. Usually fairs in the region are slower and sales happen over the course of several days,” he told ARTnews.

One of Ghiyati’s clients placed three orders on pieces ranging from $10,000 to $400,000. Within an hour of opening, dealer Sundaram Tagore had already placed two works on hold, one by Hiroshi Senju and another by Chun Kwang Young, ranging from $40,000 to $400,000. By late afternoon, Timothy Taylor had sold its entire solo presentation of paintings by Hilary Pecis to institutional and private collections in the region and internationally, to the price of $65,000-$205,000. The London-based antiquities gallery David Aaron sold a 2,000-year-old funerary stele for a seven-figure sum to a private collector, while Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects also sold out its booth of mosaic works depicting 70s-era architecture in Abu Dhabi.

Regional collectors reportedly spent big at Frieze Abu Dhabi. Iris Projects sold two works by Shamsa Al Omaira, a sculpture acquired by a new foundation in the UAE for $32,000 and an acrylic on canvas by Juma Al Haj for $20,400. UAE-based collectors also bought two ceramics by Eman Al Hashemi, priced at $17,000 and $15,000, an oil pastel on linen by Dhabia Al Qubaisi for $10,500, and a photograph by Ammar Al Attar for $12,500.

By then, Lawrie Shabibi had sold seven pieces by artists Hamra Abbas and Shaikha Al Mazrou, priced from $10,000 to $120,000. “People are recognizing the work when they’re coming here,” said the gallery’s cofounder Asmaa Al-Shabibi, referring to a new client who bought a work by Al Mazrou, who has a solo exhibition at the Cultural Foundation.

Rayan Ben El Mlih, sales and marketing manager at Waddington Custot, told ARTnews that a large contingent of collectors with reserves hailed from Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Qatar and Bahrain. The gallery brought works by Etel Adnan, Sophia Vari and Fabienne Verdier.

Dealers noted that local collectors, some of whom began their collections by acquiring Western artists, are now deepening their collections with more historical pieces by regional artists.

“We’ve been seeing European collectors diversifying their collections, too,” said Ghiyati. Dubai’s Carbon 12 sold a painting and a sculpture by 28-year-old artist Sarah Al Mehairi, as well as two works by Mexican artist Edgar Orlaineta, priced between $17,570 and $35,000 (€16,000-€32,000).

“We’ve engaged mostly with collectors that we’ve cultivated relationships with for a while, and this is our home fair,” Judy Karkour, associate director of Carbon 12, told ARTnews.

Collectors are branching out beyond SWANA this year, with notable interest in art from the African continent and its diaspora and Latin America. Meanwhile this year’s Frieze Masters section is dedicated to trade across the Indian Ocean, taking its cues from the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s current exhibition “Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean.” An hour into the fair, Efie Gallery had placed two works by Malian artist Abdoulaye Konaté on reserve, both priced between $45,000 to $65,000, in addition to two works by Cuban artist Maria Magdalena Campos Pons ($27,500-$55,000).

“Frieze Abu Dhabi has got off to a strong start for us with a high volume of enquiries in the first few hours from both institutions and private collections,” Kwame Mintah, cofounder of Efie Gallery, told ARTnews, which specializing in artists of African descent. “One of the more encouraging developments across the Gulf has been the gradual maturation of its collecting community, accompanied by a growing appreciation for artistic practices beyond established geographical and institutional frameworks,” he added.

At Daniel Crouch Rare Books, a private collector bought the first map to name Abu Dhabi, dated to 1832. While dealer Daniel Crouch declined to say how much the map sold for, he priced the booth’s total value between $10,073 and $1.19 million (AED 37,000 to AED 4.4 million).

“Abu Dhabi is becoming a cultural hub in the region with a lot of development,” Crouch said. “It’s the logical place to come to for dealing in the larger Indian Ocean region and the Louvre Abu Dhabi exhibition has attracted quite a lot of attention—we’ve obviously jumped into it with alacrity.” London-based antiquities gallery ArtAncient, carrying pieces ranging from $5,000 to $5 million, sold a collection of shipwreck jewels for an undisclosed sum—the gallery also had a visit from Venus Williams, who was admiring the Graeco-Roman mummy portrait Portrait L, which had recently been dubbed the “Mona Lisa of the Middle East.”

Throughout the opening, the blue-chip-leaning powerhouses, including Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddaeus Ropac, and Victoria Miro, boasted crowded booths. Gagosian’s dedicated Roy Lichtenstein booth became the step and repeat for many visitors—the gallery said it “placed many” orders without revealing specifics.

Judging by its debut, Abu Dhabi has become a no-brainer stop on the art fair calendar. The emirate is slowly integrating into the art circuit. Earlier this month, Christie’s hosted its first fine art auction there, with Sotheby’s own version due next month, joining a colorful lineup of events that includes the Formula 1 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Finance Week and Culture Summit Abu Dhabi.

Several dealers cited the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi’s upcoming December opening with the strong pull to participate in Frieze Abu Dhabi, characterizing the museum as a bridge between West and East.

“The Guggenheim is going to open now in the next few weeks, it’s literally where contemporary art gets space to breathe and to grow,” said Milo Gatti, fair coordinator at Galleria Continua.

#9113. SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

It is part of a wider renovation SOM announced for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

#9112. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Last medically reviewed on June 27, 2024

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Pair either with the Chase Freedom Unlimited or Chase Freedom Flex to funnel everyday spending into the UR ecosystem before converting to Hyatt points when you have a target booking.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Why this ranks among the best travel rewards redemptions

Park Hyatt is Hyatt's top-tier luxury brand, competing directly with Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, and Aman resorts. What makes this a travel rewards sweet spot is the disconnect between cash prices and points cost. While competitors like Marriott Bonvoy may charge 85,000-100,000 points for comparable luxury, Hyatt keeps Park Hyatt redemptions at Category 7-8 (25,000-30,000 points). Combined with the 1:1 transfer ratio from Chase Ultimate Rewards, a single Chase Sapphire Preferred sign-up bonus can fund multiple nights of genuine luxury.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Earn Chase Ultimate Rewards through the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or business cards like the Ink Preferred. A single sign-up bonus often covers 2-3 Park Hyatt nights. Alternatively, earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Log into your Chase account and transfer Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are typically instant, so you can transfer right before booking. Only transfer what you need for confirmed availability.

Use the World of Hyatt website or app to search your desired Park Hyatt property and dates. Filter by "Points" to see award availability. Check flexible date ranges to find the best redemption opportunities.

Complete the booking using your Hyatt points. Make sure you are logged into your World of Hyatt account so elite benefits apply. Consider booking a standard room and requesting a suite upgrade at check-in if you have Globalist status.

If you have Globalist status, contact the hotel before arrival to request suite upgrades and confirm breakfast inclusion. Even without top-tier status, joining World of Hyatt (free) earns you base-level benefits and points on incidental spend.

The fastest path is through Chase Ultimate Rewards. Cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve earn Ultimate Rewards that transfer 1:1 to World of Hyatt. A single sign-up bonus of 60,000-75,000 points can cover 2-3 nights at a Park Hyatt. You can also earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Compared to other luxury hotel chains, Park Hyatt availability is relatively good. Booking 3-6 months in advance for popular properties like Park Hyatt Tokyo or Park Hyatt Maldives improves your chances. Off-peak and shoulder season dates often have wide-open availability.

Yes. Globalist elite status works at all Park Hyatt properties and unlocks suite upgrades (subject to availability), free breakfast, late checkout, and waived resort fees. This dramatically increases the total value of a points stay.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#9110. Adobe’s democratisation of design doesn’t have to be the death of human creativity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design. While post-MAX clarity has calmed the excitement of Sneaks and new Adobe software announcements, an uncertain existentialism still lingers. Finally, everyone has the freedom to create, but in the same breath, oh dear... everyone has the freedom to create.

Add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon. Throughout MAX, I am constantly assured AI is only there for those who want it, but I'm also hyperaware that its siren song is far too tempting for certain creatives. It all boils down to one question. In the age of democratised creativity, what defines real design?

MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone. Whether you're a novice creative looking to jazz up a poster, a seasoned influencer wanting clickworthy content or an industry vet trying to adapt to the ever-demanding creative industry, Adobe is, by its own positioning, your best friend.

This is where cracks already begin to form. Classically trained graphic designers, web developers and old-school content creators who learned through education or self-taught graft are left feeling cheated while new-gen creatives have it all at their fingertips. It's not childish to feel that things are a little unfair. There is value to the blood, sweat and tears of art created over time – something AI appears to extinguish.

And while on the surface, creativity for everyone feels like a utopian dream, the addition of AI makes me worried. Of course, jobs are sacrificed under the guise of saving time and budget, and when everyone can create, where do we find value in creativity?

Can a concept half-baked by a computer hold the same emotional nuance as human-made work? I fall in the camp of no. But art has always been subjective – who's to say an AI-generated design has less value when, at its core, it was sparked by a human idea? A better question is, where do we draw the line?

It's easy to make Adobe the fall guy for the rise in AI slop, but it's just as much a matter of how we use its tools. At Sneaks, I witnessed a number of genuinely innovative tools, like Project Deep Brush – an AI-powered lighting-aware tool for Photoshop – that proved there's a distinct difference between full-send gen AI and the odd tool to make your everyday workflow a little smoother. Adobe developers aren't sitting in front of an evil AI cauldron preying on the downfall of human design as we know it. Behind the scenes, there are glimmers of hope.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

If used in a measured way, I believe AI tools can be an extension of creativity, but with no constraint other than the moral, and Adobe churning out corner-cutting AI tools with reckless abandon, it's no surprise there's slop everywhere. New creatives are hungry to push the confines of what creativity can be – AI is proposed to them as a wacky friend that can do it all. The role of 'creative' is in a state of flux, and with a new generation redefining what creativity means, artistic value has never been more abstract.

A repeated argument for Adobe's influx of AI innovations was the creative industry's increasing demand for content. A graphic designer may now be expected to be a master of motion design, web development and social media with fewer resources and even less time. These tools are merely a part of evolution – embrace them or get left behind.

But from the sidelines, I watch in horror as the creative industry eats itself over and over again. More content requires faster output. Faster output is aided by time-saving AI tools. Saved time means more space to create more content to feed the hungry attention economy. We're creating more, but as a result, we're losing a sense of quality and control. And when creativity is democratised, I worry valuable work gets lost in the shuffle.

I worry I'm a snob – that my jaded opinions are stuck in a creative world that no longer exists – but despite my discomfort, I remain hopeful. Creative democracy has its value. Accessibility is better than ever (given you can afford an Adobe subscription), and voices that may not have had the confidence to create are now empowered to do so thanks to Adobe's tools.

But what of the classic designer, like my father, who has spent decades curating their craft, only to have AI do it in seconds? It's an uncomfortable reality, but change is inevitable. To the jaded, fearful or downright nihilistic creative, I implore you to continue creating on your own terms, whether that means dipping a toe into AI tools or outright denunciation of the technology. Amidst the formulaic sea of AI, it's the quality, human-made content that will be celebrated.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

#9109. The Landing, Beloved Los Angeles Gallery with a Keen Eye for Pairing Historical and Contemporary Artists, Closes After 14 Years

The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was defined by its unique pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced that it had closed. Its last exhibition was a one-night only solo for Maxwell Hendler staged on October 29.

On the gallery’s website, founder and owner Gerard O’Brien wrote, “the Landing Gallery at 5118 W Jefferson Blvd is now closed. We are no longer programming at this location. We are deeply grateful to the artists, collectors, collaborators, and community who have been fellow participants in our engagements. It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery.” Related Articles Two More Vienna Galleries Close, Citing 'No New Collectors' and 'Challenging' Financial Landscape Prairie, Chicago Gallery That Put Conceptualism Ahead of Commercialism, Closes After Nearly a Decade

In an Instagram post, Gerard O’Brien put it more simply, “End of an era … 22 years of Gallery spaces in Los Angeles, Reform Galley 2004-2019 … the Landing Gallery 2012 -2026 … onwards. thank you Los Angeles❣️”

O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an off-shoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of the distinction between art and design. He chose the name for its original location, a spot within Reform: “he cleared out the landing atop a short staircase in his furniture gallery and dedicated it to shows of art, bringing in work by artists both contemporary and historical to display just above his design wares,” as a 2016 blog post by book publisher Phaidon reported.

In 2015, O’Brien decided that it was time for the Landing to grow, opening in a 2,800-square-foot gallery space on Jefferson Boulevard with a solo show for the late California artist JB Blunk.

Over the years, the Landing would become known for its pairings of historical and contemporary artists. At the time of its closing, its roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living contemporary artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez).

The gallery was also known for regularly staging off-kilter group exhibitions, with titles like “Rat Bastard Protective Association” (2016), “The Useful and the Decorative” (2017), “New Iconography: Artists Raising Children” (2021), and “Consensual Ennui (2023). The first of these, “3 Women” (2016) took its name from a 1977 Robert Altman film as a way “to create a cross-generational dialogue that explores the intersections of craft and fine art, influence and homage,” per a release. It featured the work of Lenore Tawney from the 1960s and ’70s paired with textile pieces by Tanya Aguiñiga and paintings by Loie Hollowell. The exhibition marked the first time Tawney’s work had been exhibited in LA in nearly 50 years.

In an Artforum review, Erin Kimmel wrote, “The Landing’s handsome, restrained exhibition showcased the exquisite detail of [Tawney’s] works, which reward prolonged scrutiny with seemingly boundless formal revelations.”

To mark its 10th anniversary at its Jefferson Boulevard space, the Landing mounted a two-part anniversary exhibition. The first part, which opened in November 2025, focused on contemporary art and design and featured the work of Ruth Asawa, Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Lyne Foulkes, and Doyle Lane. The second part, which opened this past April, featured gallery artists as well as others who had exhibited there, including Brenda Goodman, Sam Jablon, and Lukas Geronimas.

In a release for part one, O’Brien wrote, “10 Year brings together the feeling of the earliest days of the Landing Gallery when two years of exhibitions took place inside Reform Gallery on Melrose Avenue. Exhibiting art in a salon style in dialogue with decorative arts is how tL began.”

The Landing’s closure is the latest in an extended wave of closures that began in mid-2025. Los Angeles galleries have particularly been affected, with Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, and Blum all shuttering, along with the LA outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar.

In his statement on the gallery’s website, O’Brien added, “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future offsite exhibitions, activations, and special projects. Thank you for being part of the Landing’s ongoing narrative.”

#9108. Christie’s Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy

By Brian Boucher, Harrison Jacobs November 19, 2026 10:49pm

Christie’s finished out New York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.

The sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved New York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million. Related Articles Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie's Day Sale

After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.

Many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.

The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.

The most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.

Also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.

Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.)

Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.

The hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.

The large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.

Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.

The 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.

There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.

“The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”

Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”

On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).

The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it quickly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.

The sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

#9107. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

#9106. Perron shapes Quebec kitchen around tea collection

A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” said Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her.”

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” said Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” said the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

#9104. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024
