#9074. air-powered vehicles take passengers on a journey beneath the water’s surface

developed by sub sea systems, the attraction combines a gravity-fed track, an air-powered propulsion system, and enclosed passenger cabins to create a new kind of aquatic entertainment.

Sub Sea Systems’ Aquaticar is an underwater adventure ride that takes water park visitors beneath the surface in small, enclosed submersible vehicles. Developed by the company’s Sub Sea Creative division, the attraction is designed to bring a different dimension to aquatic entertainment, combining a gravity-fed course, an air-powered propulsion system, and an immersive underwater environment. The first installation is now open at Aquarabia Water Theme Park, where visitors travel through a themed underwater landscape without needing to swim or dive.

Aquaticar places passengers directly beneath the water. Two guests board each vehicle before a transparent canopy closes over the cabin. The cars then descend along a submerged track, traveling past artificial reefs, shipwrecks, and aquatic scenery, with fish and stingrays forming part of the designed environment. Passengers remain dry from the chest upward while moving through the underwater course.

Sub Sea Systems’ patented Bubble Engine, a propulsion system that uses compressed air, plumbs integrated beneath the track and supplies air through specialized triggers, releasing bubbles underneath passing vehicles and propelling them along the course.

The system is designed around a 137-meter circuit, with a ride lasting approximately 6.8 minutes. According to the manufacturer, the attraction can accommodate up to 300 guests per hour, depending on its operating configuration.

The use of air as a propulsion medium shapes the safety infrastructure of the ride. Sub Sea Systems describes a redundant air supply and communication system, with fresh air continuously circulated inside the passenger cabins. Emergency provisions include multiple levels of Emergency Air Supply, an independent onboard air supply, and an airbag system intended to bring vehicles back to the water’s surface. The manufacturer also states that the ride is TÜV SÜD certified.

#9073. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#9071. podcast: indian architects ask who shapes homes: algorithms or occupants

the conversations trace how aesthetic ideals travel between public feeds and the private home, debating who determines an ideal environment: algorithms, designers, or the occupants themselves.

Continuing the Room for Utopias podcast series produced with INDX|GLOBAL, designboom presents its fifth feature. Following discussions in Paris that tackled site listening, dismantled signature styles, and turned outdated bylaws into habitable spaces, this installment investigates the criteria that shape our concept of beauty. Hosted by designboom managing Editor, Iñaki Laguardia, two panel conversations bring together seven Indian architects and interior designers to examine the fifth series theme, The Worlds We Call Beautiful. The conversations trace how aesthetic ideals travel between public feeds and the private home, debating who determines an ideal environment: algorithms, designers, or the occupants themselves.

Satyadeep Sonar of Creations & Urban Saints opens the tenth episode by confronting the gap between online image consumption and regional thermal performance. While digital algorithms circulate smooth, stylized interiors internationally, they strip out environmental context. ‘I tell my clients: ‘You are seeing the picture, but you’re not seeing the temperature… so you better take a call on that aspect as well,’‘ Sonar explains. Sonar argues that while online aesthetic trends cycle weekly, buildings remain in place for decades. Gayatri Gunjal of Yellow Sub Studio positions the architect as a selective filter, noting that the most rigorous phase of a project involves stripping away superficial digital references to arrive at durable, context-driven layouts.

Priya Doon of The Picturesque Studio explains how residential commissions reconcile long-term construction with shifting domestic tastes. Doon argues that heavy building envelopes demand architectural permanence, whereas transient styling belongs in adaptable, movable layers. ‘The larger, massive buildings stay permanent, and infusing trends into something which is more… movable, like the art or the furniture or the rugs… that is something which is ever-evolving,‘ Doon notes. For Doon, the quality of a space rests on human emotion and daily sensation rather than abstract technical benchmarks.

Gunjal points out that Indian practices have access to extensive artisanal knowledge that is often overlooked when studios replicate Western imagery. Gunjal advocates for working directly with regional craft guilds and vernacular building systems, stating that spatial character develops through local material intelligence. Sonar reinforces this stance, observing that resilient design emerges when interior layouts adjust to changing climatic conditions across the year rather than relying on decorative surfaces.

The eleventh episode turns toward the residence as a personal sanctuary. Love Choudhary of AND Studio questions domestic plans configured primarily for public performance or external photography. ‘We should be thinking of designing homes that are not for performance—they are to be lived in, they have to be felt…‘ Choudhary states, noting that architectural framing must step back to let household routines occupy the foreground. In contrast, Reettika Puri of Y Tre Dezeen observes that clients deliberately request expressive entertaining zones for hosting guests. Puri argues that while public reception rooms can support calculated visual drama, utilitarian discipline must govern how private quarters operate.

Kushal Gopanaboina of Studio KXS questions whether maximizing physical ease produces passive domestic environments. Gopanaboina suggests that introducing calculated spatial friction encourages conscious interaction between an inhabitant and the building. ‘Discomfort is the respect you give the design, and comfort is where you don’t put your mind,‘ Gopanaboina observes, describing bedrooms as neutral canvases that occupants alter through daily occupation. Priyanka Singh of Chalk Studio applies this principle to the drafting process, explaining that studios must push through moments of creative resistance to produce responsive, characterful spaces.

The discussion concludes with reflections on what future domestic architecture must protect. Singh urges designers to leave square footage unassigned, creating capacity for habits and milestones that have not yet occurred. ‘How about keeping some space in that home for life that is yet to happen?‘ Singh asks. Choudhary supports this position, noting that houses should offer occupants room to pause rather than dictating an unyielding program of activities. Puri concludes that stripping away rigid functional titles from rooms allows spaces to evolve over decades, keeping homes resilient through continuous daily use.

podcast: Room for Utopias episodes: 10 and 11

host: Iñaki Laguardia speakers: Priya Doon (The Picturesque Studio | @picturesque.studio.design), Gayatri Gunjal (Yellow Sub Studio | @yellowsubstudio), Satyadeep Sonar (Creations & Urban Saints | @creationsbyshilpisonar), Priyanka Singh (Chalk Studio | @chalkstudio.design), Love Choudhary (AND Studio | @andstudio274), Reettika Puri (Y Tre Dezeen | @ytre_dezeen), Kushal Gopanaboina (Studio KXS | @studio_kxs)

#9070. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#9069. CLB Architects creates ADU in Wyoming with rock-climbing wall

US studio CLB Architects has completed an accessory dwelling unit called Wiley, which features an outdoor climbing wall and compact living quarters for an empty-nester couple.

The small building stands on a one-acre site in Wilson, Wyoming, located just beyond the popular ski town of Jackson. The site is dotted with mature trees and sits along the west bank of the Snake River.

Before the project’s inception, the clients had lived on the property for 25 years – in a modest, 1960s house they had renovated – and had raised their son there.

As their son neared graduation from high school, the couple decided to build an ADU on the property and make it their full-time residence, while renting out the main residence.

“The new house would allow them to remain on the land they had known for decades, while experiencing it in a new way – closer to nature, with stronger connections to light, views and outdoor living,” said Jackson-based CLB Architects.

The house also represents a way to accommodate a growing need for housing while preserving the natural landscape.

“In our region, there’s a clear need for this housing type, which is economical, compact and responsive to place,” said CLB Architects partner Eric Logan.

A primary challenge for the design team was to ensure the house “met the couple’s programmatic and budget constraints” within a very compact footprint. Per country regulations, the new house could not exceed 1,000 square feet (92.9 square metres).

The architects conceived a simple, rectangular volume that rises two levels and is topped with a gabled roof. The house was carefully sited so it would feel separate from the main residence.

“Siting the building toward the back of the parcel and introducing new landscaping and tree plantings created a soft buffer between the two dwellings,” the architect said.

The team carved out portions of the exterior to form inset terraces, along with a climbing wall that is used by the couple’s son while home from college. On the east-facing elevation, a boxy protrusion forms a balcony.

Both inside and out, the team opted for materials that were durable, cost-efficient and complemented the building’s form. Dark corrugated metal clads most of the building, while tight-knot cedar was used for inset areas to provide “warmth and depth”.

The ground level contains a spacious garage for vehicles and outdoor gear. The upper level holds two bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms, all of which are organised around a central living area.

“Locating the main living spaces on the second floor allows the interiors to engage the tree canopy while maximising natural light, offering a more intimate relationship with the landscape,” the team said.

The living area opens onto a west-facing deck, which acts as an “outdoor living room” for much of the year. Large, sliding glass doors diminish the boundary between inside and out and usher in breezes during summer months.

The clients, both of whom have deep experience in design and construction fields, poured themselves into the project. The husband served as the general contractor and engaged local tradespeople to help out.

“A true labor of love, the couple built much of the house themselves, working on the construction every evening and on weekends,” the team said, noting the project was completed in about nine months.

The project offers ideas for how communities in the Mountain West can accommodate growth while preserving the natural landscape.

“With rising land values and the need to accommodate more residents, homes like this – that are compact, efficient, and contextual – can provide more housing while preserving open space,” the team said.

“As local communities grapple with growth, projects like this suggest one path forward.”

Other ADUs in America include a small, cedar-clad dwelling in California’s wine country by Schwartz and Architecture, and a compact, metal-clad building in Austin by North Arrow Studio that resembles a birdhouse.

#9068. interview: meeting the soft, breathing creatures of katrijn westland

through touch, movement, and unexpected gestures, the designer explores how textile creatures can change our relationship with everyday materials.

Katrijn Westland’s Soft Companions brings together knitted textiles, natural dyes, sensors, and pneumatic systems to create a collection of creature-like objects that breathe, move, emit warmth, and respond to touch. Developed through the Dutch designer’s background in scenography and interaction design, the project considers what happens when design stops looking at materials as passive objects and treats them as entities with behaviors that invite human attention and care.

Westland creates an ecology of sensory-responsive companions that invite us to reconsider how we relate to the material world. Her interest in this relationship starts with textiles. We are in constant contact with them, through the clothes we wear and the fabrics we touch every day, but she sees much more potential in the way they can respond to us.

Her background in multisensory scenography, working with materials, textures, scent, flavor, and movement, made her curious about how a material’s behavior can shape an experience. This curiosity now informs her work with textiles that move, react to touch, and invite interaction. ‘Soft Companions emerged from bringing these interests together, exploring how knitted textiles could become something other than passive materials, inviting sensory interaction and acts of care,’ she tells designboom.

Through Soft Companions, Westland questions why care is so often associated with living beings and whether it might also extend to the materials around us. Washing, repairing, brushing, and preserving them are understood as forms of maintenance, practical actions intended to extend the lifespan of an object. The textile and interaction designer proposes looking at these gestures differently, particularly in a culture where material relationships are many times organized around consumption and replacement. ‘What interests me about the notion of reciprocity is that it asks us to pay attention,’ she explains. ‘Rather than expecting a material to simply fulfill our needs, we might start noticing its qualities, responding to its behavior, and adjusting our own actions accordingly.’

Westland gives her textiles seemingly lifelike behaviors to investigate whether people might develop a sense of responsibility towards something they would ordinarily consider an inanimate material. Could we become attached to a textile creature, feel protective of it, or even become frustrated with it? She draws an interesting parallel with Gary Dahl’s Pet Rock (1975), which presented an ordinary stone as a pet, complete with instructions for its care. By assigning an unexpected role to something seemingly inanimate, the project exposed how easily human behavior can change when the context surrounding an object changes.

The companions communicate through a vocabulary of movement and sensation. Some breathe, purr, vibrate, or warm the body, while others respond to touch or environmental conditions. The designer is interested in understanding how combinations of familiar characteristics can evoke a sense of liveliness. ‘A question that often comes up is, “Why isn’t it a cat?”’ Katrijn Westland shares. ‘But giving something the appearance of a cat also creates expectations about how it should behave and how we should interact with it.’  These creatures suggest something living without defining what they are or how people should approach them. Their behaviors become a kind of sensory language. Purring, for instance, is commonly associated with comfort and contentment, while changes in breathing rhythms can indicate calmness, restlessness, or anxiety. The absence of familiar facial expressions leaves these interpretations open.

Westland’s approach also draws on research into how people attribute intentions and emotions to non-human forms. In An Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior (1944), psychologists Fritz Heider and Marianne Simmel demonstrated how viewers assign intentions and emotions to simple moving geometric shapes. More recently, Kensho Miyoshi’s Designing Objects in Motion: Exploring Kinaesthetic Empathy (2020) examines how people experience the movement of non-human objects through their bodies. Textiles introduce another dimension to this relationship. Their softness and flexibility mean that movement is not only something to observe but something that can also be experienced through physical contact.

An unexpected discovery during prototyping was that imperfection could make an object feel more alive. Early works were technically clumsy, but their awkward movements made them more endearing. In one experiment, Westland attached very long textile hairs to a Roomba, which gradually became entangled in them as it moved around. ‘As it moved around, it slowly became entangled in its own hair, almost as though it were eating itself,’ she recalls. ‘Peers immediately wanted to intervene and help it get unstuck.’

With Soft Companions, Katrijn Westland considers the qualities, limitations, and behaviors of materials as active contributors to the design process. Knitted structures, for instance, can stretch, curl, fold, or resist in unexpected ways. The designer uses these characteristics as starting points for experimentation. A particular knitted structure might suggest a new movement, while a pneumatic mechanism might require a lighter or more flexible textile. The creatures are developed around three interconnected elements: their skin and muscles, bones, and heart. Their skins consist of knitted structures made from different yarn combinations, natural dyes, and textile treatments. Pneumatic or mechanical structures form their bones, enabling movement and transformation, while a small printed circuit board connects sensors and actuators to activate their behaviors.

In our conversation, Westland points to the historical connections between textile production and computing, from the punched-card system of the Jacquard loom, which influenced early computer programming, to the core rope memory of the Apollo Guidance Computer, whose software instructions were physically woven into memory modules. With Soft Companions, she brings these histories together through a contemporary application of e-textiles, combining traditional material knowledge with responsive systems. ‘Rather than letting the technology overpower the material, I’m interested in how the two can enhance one another, creating new possibilities for movement, sensory expression, and interaction while retaining the textile’s own character,’ she explains.

While their movements can suggest a sense of autonomy, much of the companions’ character becomes apparent through physical interaction.‘There is a big difference between seeing something breathe and actually holding it while it expands and contracts against your body,’ Katrijn Westland highlights. Touch is particularly important because it is inherently reciprocal. When we touch a material, we are simultaneously being touched by it. Its texture, temperature, resistance, and movement influence our physical responses, shaping how we approach and interact with it.

During testing, certain textures encouraged people to stroke or groom the creatures, while their movements prompted users to adjust their actions. Westland also discovered that the context of an encounter could significantly influence how people responded. The way a creature was introduced, the language used to describe it, and the environment in which it was placed all contributed to the interaction. When the companions were put up for adoption, people began developing individual relationships with them. Their sensory responses were far from universal. What one person experienced as comforting or calming could feel unpleasant or overstimulating to someone else.

‘This has made me curious about how textile qualities and behaviors could be tailored to different sensory preferences and needs,’ she tells us. Many participants even gave their creatures names, showing they had formed a personal connection with them.

Katrijn Westland sees Soft Companions as a way to explore how humans might live alongside and care for materials that are not alive. The idea is connected to a broader interest in our relationship with the non-human world, but it also comes from familiar experiences, such as looking after plants, becoming attached to everyday objects, or developing small habits around the things we use and live with. The project brings together different families of textile creatures, each with their own behaviors and preferences. Some are designed to stay close to the body, while others can become part of shared spaces at home or elsewhere. Not all of them need regular attention. Some simply remain in the background, occasionally inviting people to touch or interact with them.

For Westland, companionship does not have to be about what something can do for us. It can also grow through spending time with it, paying attention to it, and getting used to the way it behaves. She now wants to explore how people with different sensory preferences and care needs respond to the creatures. So far, the project has been developed through material experiments and tests with her peers.

Her next step is to involve a wider range of people and understand how they experience the creatures in different ways. She is also preparing to begin a new research position focused on temporal and biofabricated textile experiences, opening another direction for the questions raised by Soft Companions. ‘Where the current companions evoke a sense of liveliness through their movements and responses, I’m curious about what happens when the material itself can grow, change, age or require care in more direct ways,’ she reflects.

Rather than letting the technology overpower the material, I’m interested in how the two can enhance one another, creating new possibilities for movement, sensory expression and interaction while retaining the textile’s own character.

#9067. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#9066. Bubbly lamp by Canalside Studio among nine new products on Dezeen Showroom

A table lamp comprising a plastic base topped with five magnetically attached glowing orbs is among the products recently published on our Showroom section.

Magnetic connector points are placed inside the five globe-like bulbs that light this table lamp by Hong Kong-based Canalside Studio.

The Bubbly lamp comprises a statuesque base with five bulbs attached, which can be removed and positioned around a room – including attached to metal surfaces – to spread out its ambient glow.

Other products published last week include a tile collection by Ceramiche Keope, acoustic pods by Actiu and an outdoor rug range by Rima Dain.

Read on to find out about some of our latest products:

Grace Lithos tiles by Ceramiche Keope are intended to mimic the striated appearance of natural Villeneuve quartzite quarried in Italy.

As well as being striped with differently coloured striations, the tiles feature the stone’s abundance of mineral inclusions and the glinting mica microcrystals that it is studded with.

Amber and white veining streaks across the surface of Italian stone company Antolini‘s aptly-named Blueroots marble.

The slabs can be used in kitchens and bathrooms as interior cladding or to create furnishings, imbuing interiors with visually stimulating surfaces.

Office furniture brand Actiu has evolved its Qyos acoustic pods, expanding on its configuration options and capacity for personalisation.

Described by the brand as “adaptable microarchitecture”, new options include those that enhance both aesthetics and sound absorption.

Italian company Ceramiche Refin‘s latest surface draws on the faceted appearance of traditional terrazzo.

Palladia comes in a trio of colourways – Iride, Luce and Aurea – and a choice of two finishes, glossy Lucida or plain Matt.

Office brand Mute‘s Jetson acoustic pods have evolved to encompass a wider range of colourways, wall layouts and levels of transparency.

Also enhanced is the pods’ acoustic credentials, which the brand says now meets Class A acoustic standards in accordance with ISO 23351-1, allowing individuals and small groups to work and converse in a quiet environment.

A range of styles, shapes and sizes are available in the catalogue of Spanish brand Rima Dain, which specialises in outdoor rugs.

Rather than being an afterthought, the rugs aim to help zone and enhance outdoor spaces in both residential and hospitality contexts.

Enhanced and cutting-edge new features aim to make Swedish brand Asko‘s Steel Seal washing machines more seamless, hygienic and pleasant to use.

Two new signature technologies in particular feature in the new machines. Steel Seal, which substitutes rubber components for ones made of steel, and Quattro Construction 2.0, an integrated suspension system that reduces movement and resulting noise when in use.

Finnish company Framery has released an internal layout option for its One Pod, featuring a corner sofa in miniature.

One Lounge aims to make users feel at home with the cosy, thickly-padded corner seat, in place of a harder stool.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Avios are accessible from virtually every major transferable points currency:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Go to ba.com, log into your Executive Club account, and complete the award booking. You'll pay the Avios balance plus applicable government taxes and fees (typically $5–$30 for Aer Lingus partner bookings — far less than BA's own flight surcharges). Enter passenger details, select seats, and confirm.

BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance — if you want peak-adjacent dates, set a calendar reminder to search as early as possible. If your first-choice dates show no availability, try:

Let's make this concrete. It's late September — shoulder season, the absolute sweet spot for Ireland travel — and you and your partner want a 10-day trip to explore the Ring of Kerry and the Cliffs of Moher.

The Cash Reality: A round trip from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus in late September runs approximately $550–$650 per person in economy. For two people, you're looking at $1,100–$1,300 before you've spent a single euro in Ireland. That's real money.

The Avios Reality: 13,000 Avios per person, per direction. Round trip for two:

The CPP Math: At a midpoint cash value of $600 per ticket one-way, you're getting 4.6 cents per Avios — nearly triple what most travel rewards programs consider excellent value. Even at the conservative end ($300/ticket), you're at 2.3 cents per point, still well above average.

What the Experience Looks Like: Aer Lingus operates the BOS–DUB route on the Airbus A321LR — a purpose-built transatlantic narrowbody with a dedicated economy cabin, pull-out meal trays, and proper overhead bin space. The overnight flight departs Boston in the evening and arrives Dublin mid-morning, giving you a full day upon arrival. The crew is warm, the food is solid for economy, and there's no connection in London or Amsterdam burning hours off your vacation.

You land at Dublin Airport refreshed (enough), clear customs quickly through the U.S. preclearance facility — one of only a handful in the world — and you're on the road toward Killarney by noon. Your entire transatlantic crossing cost you about 26,000 Avios and $25 in taxes. The Chase Sapphire Preferred welcome bonus alone is worth 60,000 Ultimate Rewards points. This trip is already nearly free before you've optimized anything else.

Amex Membership Rewards periodically runs a 30% transfer bonus to British Airways Avios. When this promotion is live, your 13,000 Avios only costs you approximately 10,000 Amex points. For a family of four round trip (104,000 Avios), that drops to roughly 80,000 Amex points. Set a Google alert for "Amex British Airways transfer bonus" and strike when it appears — these promotions are time-limited.

BA's award search opens 355 days in advance. If you're targeting travel in late spring (May–early June) before peak summer pricing kicks in, mark your calendar and search the moment the window opens. Award space on direct transatlantic routes gets snapped up quickly at good dates.

BA Avios allows open jaw bookings — meaning you can fly into one airport and return from another at the same Avios price. Book Boston → Dublin inbound and Shannon or Cork → Boston outbound, and now your itinerary naturally flows west to east across the country without backtracking. This is the smart traveler's move and it costs you nothing extra in Avios.

British Airways operates some transatlantic routes with a connection through London Heathrow. The moment you're on BA-operated metal, fuel surcharges of $300–$800+ get added to your booking, completely obliterating the value. Always confirm you're booking Aer Lingus flights (flight numbers beginning with EI) when using this strategy.

Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you've transferred points and haven't yet booked, make sure your BA Executive Club account sees some activity within that window. Even earning a few Avios through a BA partner (a hotel stay, a car rental, a shopping portal purchase) resets the clock.

For earning the Avios you need for this redemption, the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (transferring Chase UR to BA at 1:1) or any Amex Membership Rewards card give you the most flexibility. Both transfer instantly to BA. If you're starting from zero, a single card welcome bonus of 60,000–100,000 points covers a round trip for one to three people depending on timing.

Nonstop to Ireland for a fraction of the cash price

Aer Lingus joined the Oneworld alliance, which means British Airways Avios can book Aer Lingus-operated flights. Because BA uses distance-based pricing, the relatively short transatlantic crossing from the East Coast to Dublin (roughly 3,000-3,500 miles) prices at just 13,000 Avios each way in economy. Compare this to using American Airlines miles (30,000+ each way) or other programs for the same transatlantic flight. The distance-based chart rewards this specific geography with disproportionately low pricing, creating one of the best-value transatlantic sweet spots available.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Verify that Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from your departure city to Dublin. The strongest year-round service is from Boston and New York. Seasonal routes may only operate during summer months.

Log into your British Airways Executive Club account and search for flights from your city to Dublin using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for Aer Lingus-operated flights (flight numbers starting with EI). Check flexible dates for the best availability.

Once you find availability, transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant from Chase and Amex.

Complete the booking on ba.com. The total will show 13,000 Avios plus taxes and surcharges (typically $50-$100 each way). Review the total out-of-pocket before confirming to make sure it meets your value threshold.

Add your Aer Lingus or Oneworld frequent flyer number to earn status credits. Remember that Dublin offers U.S. Preclearance for return flights — a significant time-saver. Consider booking accommodations using hotel points for a fully points-funded trip.

Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from Boston (BOS), New York (JFK), Newark (EWR), Hartford (BDL), Philadelphia (PHL), Washington Dulles (IAD), Chicago (ORD), and other seasonal routes. Boston and New York have the most frequent service year-round.

Aer Lingus awards do carry fuel surcharges, typically $100-$200 round trip in economy. While not zero, this is still dramatically less than the $500-$1,000+ cash fare. The net savings remain substantial despite the surcharges.

Dublin can serve as an excellent gateway to the rest of Europe. Aer Lingus offers connections to many European cities from Dublin, and you can also book separate budget airline flights within Europe. Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: New members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.

#9064. NIKE rethinks air cushioning with digitally printed patterns inside its soles

instead of relying on conventional internal supports, the sportswear company uses selective lamination to control underfoot response, with the first running models expected in late 2027.

NIKE has found another use for ink, and this time it has little to do with logos or graphics. The company has introduced Tuned Air, a manufacturing process that uses digitally applied ink to determine how different sections of an air-filled sole behave under pressure. Presented on November 16, 2026, the technology changes the internal construction of NIKE’s familiar Air units rather than introducing an entirely new cushioning material. The idea is to control which areas compress, which remain firmer and how the sole responds to movement.

Traditional NIKE Air units rely on internal pins and rigid sections to maintain their shape, a construction method that also limits how their geometry can be adjusted. Tuned Air offers an alternative by allowing engineers to create different internal configurations without depending on those fixed structures. This means that the properties of an Air unit can be adjusted across its length, potentially producing different sensations beneath the heel and forefoot. Nike intends to adapt these configurations to different sports and athletes, although the company has yet to demonstrate how the technology performs in a commercially available shoe.

The process combines proprietary digital ink with selective lamination. Ink is applied to specific areas inside an Air unit, preventing those sections from bonding during manufacturing. Areas without ink, meanwhile, are joined together. By controlling this pattern, engineers can determine the geometry of the internal structure and influence how it compresses and rebounds. Rather than assembling a different mechanical configuration for every variation, NIKE can modify the printed pattern to produce different cushioning characteristics.

The inspiration came, somewhat unexpectedly, from the glossy colors of magazine covers. NIKE’s engineers began exploring how printing techniques could be adapted to create internal structures within an Air unit, eventually developing an ink-based process refined over more than a decade. The method also reduces the constraints traditionally associated with the height and shape of the units, giving designers greater freedom to experiment with their proportions. What looks like a relatively simple printed pattern is doing much of the work previously assigned to physical supports.

The manufacturing process also changes how NIKE develops its prototypes. According to the company, average development times for new Air units have fallen by 70 percent at its Advanced Product Creation Center. A prototype that previously took three weeks can now be produced in three days. This allows engineers to test more variations of internal geometry without having to redesign the entire structure each time. Nike also says the process makes it easier to reproduce specific cushioning properties across different shoe sizes, although these improvements remain company-reported figures.

The first Tuned Air running shoes are scheduled to arrive in late 2027, with applications in other sports and NIKE Sportswear planned to follow. The technology was previewed at NIKE’s World of Athletes event through a series of colorful components illustrating the possible internal configurations. No specific commercial models or independent performance results have been announced. For the moment, the most interesting part of NIKE’s latest footwear experiment is something that will be largely invisible once the shoe is on someone’s foot.

#9062. Programa software tracks everything from product dimensions to material quantities

Studio operations software Programa has redesigned its programme to rethink how interior design studios operate, giving practices more flexibility and freeing up their time.

According to Programa, beautiful interiors are built on “hundreds of decisions”, which take long periods of time to decide upon and update across multiple spreadsheets.

Each decision brings specification details, quantities, pricing and revisions that studios must keep updated as a project develops.

These include minute, precise details such as dimensions, materials, finishes, technical requirements, and component quantities.

Programa‘s redesigned programme keeps a record of each item used in an interior project, from furniture and lighting to hardware and finishes, and optimises their organisation based on how the project runs.

The company explained that increased AI use is making convincing images “easier to generate than ever”, yet clients often run into logistical issues when using this alone.

For example, the AI model doesn’t take into account whether a wardrobe or sofa fits through the door, suits the needs of the people living there, or whether the overall design takes full advantage of a space’s natural light.

With Programa, the designer can smoothly make these judgements using the software’s organisation of specifications, cost, quantities and overall project coordination.

The company explained that if a designer updates a product’s shared specification once, the change appears in the Programa schedules that include it, while quantities can be individually allocated by room.

For Austin Carrier of Californian design studio, Hommeboys Interiors, this is particularly helpful.

“We use schedules for everything from lighting and hardware to plumbing fixtures and furniture, indoor and outdoor,” Carrier explained.

“For furniture, we can break down every room, then the pieces within that room, and give clients several options to reject or accept,” he added.

As a result, the software aims to cut the “gruelling amount of work” updating schedules, preparing presentations, and communicating with suppliers. It also reduces repeated data entry, freeing up time.

The platform is defined as an “alternative to spreadsheets”, which often have to be made from scratch and reformatted for different presentations.

“The issue with the spreadsheet is that it’s like a blank cell,” added Los Angeles-based designer Paul Chan. “You can put anything in there – it doesn’t carry from one project to another.”

“With Programa, I can take a format from one project and move it into the next,” Chan continued. “There’s consistency between each project.”

Specifically, the Programa Schedule function details the items’ code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

It offers a streamlined place to reference drawings, get client approval and work with contractors to meet on-site deadlines.

The company explained that one of its platform’s main benefits is that it can be used from early product decision-making through to final delivery.

Here, the studio manages the specification and controls what is shared, whereas the clients review selections and provide approvals. Collaborators also receive the information relevant to their work.

“Once we get all of the information in there, we can send it out in one email to all of our vendors, and then they are able to get us pricing back very easily,” added Tana Nesbitt-Hayes of Studio 8 Architect.

“If we’re exceeding our budget in one area, we can tailor it back. It’s always up-to-date.”

“We share our Programa Schedules with the millworkers and the engineers,” she added. “They can see the refrigerator we’re going to put in, and they can make the panels to fit.”

Programa offers a free trial for all studios. To learn more, visit its website.

#9061. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#9060. perkins&will and estúdio campana wrap são paulo airport lounge in amazon river-inspired timber installation

inside terminal 3 of são paulo’s guarulhos international airport, perkins&will and estúdio campana design the 1,400-sqm pedra preta lounge, anchored by a curved timber entrance installation modeled on the amazon’s juruá river and espírito santo stone interiors.

Perkins&Will edited by christina vergopoulou November 19, 2026 3 min

The spatial progression begins at the entrance, where a sculptural timber installation by Brazilian practice Estúdio Campana, modeled on the meandering curves of the Amazon’s Juruá River, wraps the reception area to form a physical and acoustic threshold from the surrounding terminal. Inside, Perkins&Will studio employs curved transitions, layered lighting, and framed sightlines to delineate zones while maintaining orientation toward departure gates. The material palette pairs natural stone quarried in Espírito Santo with warm timber, textured wall finishes, and custom-designed furnishings that integrate built-in architecture with furniture. A curated selection of Brazilian modern and contemporary artworks is embedded throughout the circulation path rather than isolated in gallery displays, complemented by a hospitality program featuring menus by chef Luiz Filipe Souza and wine pairings curated by sommelier Juliana Carani.

#9059. Seaweed earplug among grant-winning Design Museum prototypes

A single-use earplug crafted from seaweed, two plant-based insulation materials and a homegrown timber kit-of-parts for low-rise buildings are among the projects that have been awarded Design Museum grants.

UK-based studios Searo Labs, WeCanMake, Local Works Studio and SY Ecofit have been granted a share of £280,000 from the Design Museum for their “cutting-edge” environmental prototypes.

Described as the “world’s first seaweed-based single-use earplug”, SearoSoft by Cambridge-based Searo Labs is a fully biodegradable and renewable alternative to single-use earplugs.

According to SearoSoft, the soft, mouldable earplugs are made without microplastics or chemicals and designed to hydrate the ear canal, unlike plastic-based products, which can be drying.

Once discarded, they are biodegradable in water or soil after 30 days. As seaweed is a regenerative crop, SearoSoft explained that there is no need for land, freshwater or fertilisers, making the process simple and more sustainable.

Among the other prototypes is a building material project by Sussex-based Local Works Studio. The initiative, named Ferment, will repurpose agricultural waste into an insulating material fit for retrofitting buildings.

Local Works Studio aims to develop an accessible product for farms via what it calls a “harvest-to-house system”, where farmers can produce the insulation themselves using their existing infrastructure, skills and machinery.

Bristol-based studio WeCanMake’s winning prototype, Neighbourhood Factory Futures, is a homegrown timber kit-of-parts system designed to be used for constructing low-rise apartment buildings.

With the Design Museum’s grant, the studio plans to create a neighbourhood factory model, allowing local communities to build and maintain their own homes.

WeCanMake explained it created the system as part of a wider movement aiming to make the UK a “nation of growers, producers and makers” while using reusable materials that store, rather than emit, carbon.

Prototyping PhytoFloc by social enterprise SY Ecofit in collaboration with Phyona and Studio Bio is a zero-waste project that, similarly to Local Works Studio, aims to develop plant-based insulation for building construction.

The project uses biowaste created as a byproduct of phytomining, where former industrial land is rejuvenated by plants that extract pollutants from the soil.

The project intends to recognise the value of post-industrial soils while creating a locally made, low-carbon material.

The grants are part of the Design Museum’s Future Observatory program, which is run in partnership with the Arts and Humanities Research Council. The winning projects were amongst 140 prototypes that were submitted to the scheme.

The museum explained that at a time when supply chains are under pressure, the Future Observatory aims to support designers’ practical research to drive the green transition.

“The climate crisis demands rapid change, and we believe that design is critically important if we are to meet that challenge,” said Design Museum director Tim Marlow.

“The presence of Future Observatory allows us an extraordinary opportunity to get involved with practitioners and problem-solvers and have a direct impact on the development of new technologies at the frontier of current design thinking.”

The four projects will be funded from November 2026 until July 2027. Afterwards, the prototypes will be tested and begin the commercialisation process.

#9058. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024
